#876. European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome

It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant those bodies.

“Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies.

However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of the top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape.

Sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations.

The prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken faultlines in football open up,” one source says of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship.

This particularly appears the case now that, in the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs.

While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn, the latter will not be far behind.

That is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through.

Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised last year with the creation of commercial entity UC3, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino.

One source with knowledge of the discussions claims Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could be made at next month’s Fifa council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the global governing body seems more likely.

The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through.

While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, sent an explosive letter to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, on 31 July.

EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off plan was formally dropped the following day.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

One particularly incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

Al-Khelaïfi, who is also the president of Paris Saint-Germain, did not directly address the issue during his speech in Copenhagen two months later and there are suggestions a mutually beneficial solution has been reached. The crisis may have landed EFC the terms they wanted.

“It’s not a matter of whether Gianni wins [the election], but what his mandate is, and who is behind it,” a senior source in European football said. “A large part of the answer is EFC. EFC is going to take over Fifa in the same way [it] took over Uefa. The big clubs have gained yet more power and control.

“EFC initially came out very hard against Gianni, but were quick to row back. They’ve been silent on the presidential election and other governance issues, as it’s clear they’ve reached an agreement with Fifa. The joint venture is the price of their silence.”

The result is likely to be an acceleration of trends already under way. The biggest European clubs look set to make even more money from new tournaments, particularly given they are likely to increase in size and regularity, beginning with a 48-team men’s Club World Cup in 2029.

Chelsea earned $115m (£85m) from winning the inaugural expanded tournament last year, with six European clubs in the top seven of the prize money table and Brazil’s Fluminense the only non-European side to earn more than $50m. Solidarity payments are also skewed towards Europe, whose clubs will receive 50% of the $250m pot despite providing only 12 of the 32 contestants. Those defending the status quo note that Europe generates about 70% of Fifa’s revenue.

A senior source at another confederation said the inevitable result of the joint venture would be less money for the rest of the world, certainly in proportional terms. “The most significant long-term result of the Fifa crisis will be to entrench the economic might of the biggest European clubs,” they said. “That means reduced access to competitions, less revenue and broadcast rights for the rest of us.

“The European clubs are well organised, economically rational and have taken advantage of the opportunity to extract something from Fifa. Gianni Infantino is in the business of writing cheques and will now be writing big ones to clubs as well as member associations.”

These developments are, at least, easily foreseeable. It is less straightforward to analyse how football’s face will change if a putative World Football Clubs gains the power many believe lies in its sights. “Every club around the world deserves to be represented; to have a voice, and a better chance to succeed,” Al-Khelaïfi said in his September address. But the world’s wealthiest clubs stand poised to benefit from football’s crisis more handsomely than anyone.

#875. How do NI replace 'perfect player' Donley?

Northern Ireland play Hungary in Budapest needing a point for Nations League promotion

With six of his starting outfield players against Ukraine on Saturday night having gone into the game a yellow card away from suspension, it was always likely that Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill would need to reshuffle his team for the Nations League Group B2 finale in Hungary.

That the player who picked up the booking ended up being Jamie Donley, however, has presented the boss with something of a selection conundrum.

The Tottenham Hotspur forward, currently on loan at Luton Town, has started the side's past 10 games at centre-forward, a different role to the deeper position he has more usually occupied in his club career.

With O'Neill having circled through traditional number nine options such as Dion Charles, Jamie Reid and Lee Bonis since returning to the job four years ago, it feels as if Donley has made the shirt his own since being handed the start against Luxembourg 12 months ago.

While the manager has pushed back on the idea that Donley is playing out of position at international level, the one-game ban is certainly an untimely one with the former Leyton Orient and Oxford United loanee's hold-up play in particular against Ukraine showing how much he has grown into the role.

After the 21-year-old had a goal chalked off by the video assistant referee (VAR) on Saturday, he has still scored just once from open play for his country, but there is a growing appreciation that he is asked to bring much more than just goals to the team.

"He's been such a good player for us. Even without the goals, the way he holds the ball up and spreads the play, his movement is just so good. Playing balls in the air, he pins the defender so well," said Fulham midfielder Shea Charles.

"He's got better every game and he's like the perfect player for us."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC One NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

There is no obvious like-for-like replacement in O'Neill's squad for a game in which they need a draw to secure promotion to Nations League A for the first time.

Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill pulled out of the double-header through injury last week, with Josh Magennis, Callum Marshall and the uncapped pair of Eoin Kenny and Braiden Graham the other strikers in the travelling party.

Similar to the original ask of Donley, there is also an option to move a wide or deeper player such as Isaac Price or Paddy Kelly into a central striking role.

With only three days between games, however, there has been little time to work on such a plan to replace a player whose four Spurs appearances all came under Ange Postecoglou in the 2023-24 season.

"There are other things we can do. We can change the shape a little bit, play with two front players," said O'Neill, who himself is suspended for the game after two bookings and will watch from the stands.

"There's a number of things that we will look at. Obviously the time between the games makes that somewhat more difficult in terms of preparation.

"We'll find hopefully the right player that can first of all fit into what we want to do, but obviously secondly give the opposition some problems as well."

Nobody in O'Neill's squad has more international caps or goals than Stevenage striker Magennis.

But while the 36-year-old has started 11 games in League One this season, it has been more than three years since he last did so at international level.

"My role has obviously changed since I've come into the squad," said the player with 94 international appearances and 12 goals to his name.

"If Michael wants to play with the target man and with experience, obviously, he's going to go for me. If he wants a like-for-like, he's probably going to go with Marshy [Callum Marshall]. So, me and Marshy will probably play rock, paper, scissors.

"Jamie brings so much to the team, but I don't think there's going to be a drastic downfall if one of us has to step in for us. I think the competition for places in the squad for us is absolutely brilliant and if you get that opportunity, you've just got to take it."

#874. See Cardi B’s Out-of-This-World Birthday Party for Son Grey

Cardi B celebrated her and Stefon Diggs' son Grey on his first birthday with an extravagant space-themed party. The rapper—also mom to her trio with ex Offset—dubbed the bash "Grey's World."

Cardi B’s universe revolves around her kids.

And the "Bodak Yellow" rapper made that clear as she threw an over-the-top party for her youngest, Grey—her son with Stefon Diggs—to celebrate his first birthday.

"Y'all don't even understand. This look crazy in person," Cardi said while exploring the space-themed set-up in footage shared to Instagram Nov. 15, before adding "Your world, Grey!"

In addition, Cardi—also mom to kids Kulture, 8, Wave, 5 and Blossom, 2, with ex Offset—completed the lavish affair with a sushi bar and live music for her entire family to dance to. As such, the Grammy winner's sister, Hennessy Almánzar, shared the dance floor with a Transformer robot, while Cardi and the birthday boy shared a sweet moment set to salsa music.

The festivities followed the 34-year-old's birthday tribute to her son with the NFL star, in which she revealed his name after previously keeping it under wraps.

"Happy 1st birthday to Grey Marsean Diggs!!" she wrote on Instagram Nov. 4. "It’s only been 1 year since meeting you but it feels like I’ve had you at my side forever."

And the moniker is particularly meaningful for Cardi, as it reflects the journey of bringing her fourth-born into this world.

"I carried you through one of the most uncertain high pressured times of my life but having you inside of me through it all gave me a extra strength," she shared, adding, "You gave a new meaning to what a Grey day feels like. You light up my life and every room with your smile your laugh and your precious spirit."

The sweet message also showed off the toddler's clever Halloween costume, having scrubbed in as an adorable doctor from Grey's Anatomy.

And while Stefon's role at the party was kept behind the scenes, Cardi previously shared how the New England Patriot was a key part of their growing family's success.

"I'm doing all this work, but I'm doing all this work while I'm creating a baby," a then-pregnant Cardi explained on CBS Mornings, in 2025. "Me and my man, we're very supportive of each other."

Read on to revisit Cardi and Stefon's meteoric path to parenthood.

While fans already knew Cardi B likes those Balenciagas (the ones that look like socks), they began wondering if she also liked Stefon Diggs in October 2024. The rapper and the New England Patriots wide receiver then fueled dating speculation after they were photographed together on Valentine's Day 2025.Though Cardi hasn't revealed the exact Xs and Os of how she met Stefon, it was more or less her thinking, "Oh he's so handsome, what's his name?""I thought he was cute," she said on a September 2025 episode of Today, noting they connected through mutual friends. "I was like, 'Oh, he gotta be mine.'"

While some would prefer to finesse rumors, the Grammy winner and the athlete weren't afraid to keep people talking when they stepped out for a 2025 Met Gala after-party in May.

Later that month, Cardi and Stefon confirmed they're a couple while attending an NBA Playoff game between the Celtics and the Knicks in New York.

"It’s tough hiding. It’s tough dating in your 30s, too, but I like him. I love him, today," the "Bodak Yellow" artist told Billboard in September 2025.  "I was always scared of dating people [because] I’ve always been in a long relationship since I was like 21."

Cardi and Stefon seemed to be living their best life while spending Memorial Day weekend on a yacht in Miami, Fla.

In June 2025, the "Money" star and the football player made some more moves, debuting their relationship on Instagram and then taking a trip to Paris.

But fans began to wonder if Cardi and Stefon had already split after their Instagram post marking their hard launch was deleted in July 2025.However, the musician assured followers things were Okurrr after she posted a video showcasing the Patek Philippe watch she got from Stefon."My boo boo got it for me at London Jewelers," she said in an August 2025 TikTok. "You know, I went to link up with him at London Jewelers and I thought he was buying himself a watch. And [he was] like, 'Surprise, a watch for you!' And [I was like], 'Ahhh! Thank you!'"

Weeks later, there was speculation that Cardi could be growing her family. But when the star—who also shares kids Kulture, Wave and Blossom with ex Offset—was asked about the paternity of her rumored little one, she slammed the question."You’re disrespectful. Don’t do that," she told the inquirer in September 2025 while exiting a courthouse in L.A., where she won her viral trial. "Do you see women asking those types of questions to me?...Why do you feel as a man you get to ask me those types of questions? Act like you have some manners. Your mama taught you: Respect women."

Later that month, Cardi confirmed she and Stefon are expecting a baby. While the child will be the couple's first together, the bundle of joy marks her fourth and his second overall (He is dad to daughter Nova from a previous relationship)."Everybody kept telling me I should have fun, and we had a little bit of too fun and now I’m here," Cardi told CBS Mornings in September 2025, adding, "We’re very excited. We’re very happy."And she had a message for all those who had been spreading pregnancy rumors."Now y’all can buy my album so I can buy Pampers and diapers and all that type of stuff," Cardi added, referencing her sophomore release Am I the Drama?. "I told ya. Now go support my album ‘cause I’m a mother of four now."

For Cardi, forming a new relationship with Stefon after her divorce from Offset required her to be "open and vulnerable.""One time he just told me like, ‘Let me heal you,'" she continued on CBS Mornings. "'Give me a chance for me to heal you.'"And while Stefon plays offense, he's quick to come to Cardi's defense. Like when he supported her ahead of her album release."When people just rip it apart, it just hurts you and it crush you," she added. "He’s like, ‘Girl, you better get it together.’ He makes me feel very confident. I feel like feeling safe is feeling confident. Feeling like you can do it, and it makes you feel like you can take over the world."Of course, the support goes both ways as Cardi noted she's become a football fan."I be in the screen on Sunday, every day, cursing people out," she said on a September 2025 episode of Today. "'Pass the ball!'"

Shortly after Cardi announced her pregnancy, Stefon made headlines over a lawsuit model Aileen Lopera filed in December 2024 in which she accused him of fathering her baby girl born in April 2025, per court documents obtained by People. According to his response obtained by the outlet, Stefon has contested the allegation that he fathered the child and has requested genetic testing to determine paternity.Cardi then appeared to address the drama on social media."Hello, Barbara. This is Shirley," she said in a September 2025, giving a nod to the lyrics of Shirley Brown’s song "Woman to Woman" in which a woman calls up her partner’s mistress. "That’s your baby daddy, b---h? That’s my baby daddy, too. Well what now? I don’t f--king know. We’ll figure it out b---h."

#873. What's the story with Scotland boss Pocognoli - is it time to go?

A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.

The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.

The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.

They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.

For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.

Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.

Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.

A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.

Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.

Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man

Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.

There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.

In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.

In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.

'You do not have time in international football'

If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.

Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.

In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?

Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.

More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.

Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?

An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.

Pocognoli comes across as a good person: open, communicative, passionate and hard-working.

He also appears stubborn in the way he sets up his team, a system that is so easily exploited by more experienced coaches, people like Switzerland boss Murat Yakin, who was missing a battalion of heavy hitters and yet still won this game at a canter.

Yakin started six players who had six caps or fewer to their name - three of them scored.

McGinn said later that Scotland were in this movie before in the early days of Clarke's tenure, mentioning the 4-0 loss to Russia in 2019 - four goals conceded in 27 minutes.

The difference between Clarke and Pocognoli is obvious. Clarke had vast experience and the nous to fix the problems. Pocognoli is a young coach with no such back story, no such track record in turning bad situations into good.

Pocognoli said later that people should look beyond the result, to the "attitude of the players" who were at times "brilliant, brave and on the front foot".

He argued that 4-0 wasn't a true reflection of the game, referring to the glaring misses by Lewis Ferguson and Scott McTominay. Scotland were 3-0 down at the time. He didn't think the loss had anything to do with a system or a lack of confidence or a lack of belief.

Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.

After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.

McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.

Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.

To repeat Robertson's line, you don't get time.

Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.

It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.

#872. A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion.

The Ravenna manager, Andrea Mandorlini, deployed Ronaldinho in a central position, just behind the striker Simone Rabbi. The Brazilian held his position well, but was slow to get going. As the game progressed, he warmed up and showed his excellent skills; some things do not appear to change. Ronaldinho touched the ball 25 times, took three corners – one of which nearly led to a Ravenna goal – and initiated the move that led to the hosts taking the lead in the 35th minute.

Having trained with the team just once, whether he plays again remains to be seen. But he had already sprinkled some magic on a club and a region that has not made headlines in years. He played the first half as Ravenna won 2-0 to stay second in the division’s Group B (the Italian third tier is divided into three regional sections). Only the group winners earn promotion and Ravenna trail Spezia by six points.

Whatever happens for the remainder of the season this has put the club back on the football map. Ravenna’s highest finish was eighth in Serie B, in 1996-97, but this match was broadcast live by Sky Sports in Italy and shown in several other countries. It even appeared on the giant screens in New York’s Times Square, where the club’s owners, the Cipriani family, have built much of their international reputation through Harry’s Bar.

The town’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, who, as always, was watching the game from the stands, said: “A champion like Ronaldinho, a world football icon, brings great visibility and today is an opportunity for us to showcase Ravenna around the world, from our stadium. It is something new for us and together with the club the municipality will try to understand how this can have a positive impact on the town.”

The local community had been excited at the prospect of Ronaldinho representing the club, but there was some regret, too. “It would have been nice if he had come to take a stroll around the city, among the people who live here and own the shops,” the barista Barbara said before the game.

So how did he end up here? The Brazilian is a friend of Ignazio Cipriani, the owner of the Giallorossi. Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida, old acquaintances from Ronaldinho’s time at Milan, are also part of the club. They convinced him to become an investor in the club and to pull on his boots again. In addition, Ravenna are now wearing his R10 sportswear line and one of the stands bears the same name.

Ravenna are aiming high. Cipriani has never hidden the fact he is aiming for Serie A, which is ambitious for a city with a population of 156,000. And Sunday brought hope, Dinho stepping on to the pitch in a gold-trimmed kit picked by the club to celebrate his arrival (and available for sale at €120). His hair was kept in check by a black headband and he was wearing gloves on a chilly afternoon. On his back, the No 10, something more than just a number for him, the man who became a global hero thanks to his extraordinary skill and contagious smile.

A younger generation has been able to discover Ronaldinho’s genius through the endless supply of online videos showcasing his greatest moments. Children who have never seen him play know his tricks and signature moves, while their parents can relive an era of football they may feel no longer exists.

“Dad, was he strong?” a young girl asked her father as they walked hand in hand towards the stadium. “Yes, he was strong. Actually, he is strong,” he corrected himself.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

One family had left Rome at 5am and travelled the 350km north just because their son had watched Ronaldinho on YouTube and wanted to see him live. Others had travelled even further, with supporters arriving from Turkey and Canada.

Ronaldinho hahas scored 299 professional goals, but his landmark 300th on his return was not to be. However, in front of a record attendance of 6,743 the way he initiated the move for Giulio Donati’s goal was ample reward for those who had turned up. Donati made his Serie A debut on 29 August 2010 for Lecce, at San Siro, against Milan, marking the Brazilian that day.

As Ronaldinho walked off at half-time, he was surrounded by a media scrum. After the game, he spoke of his desire to play again. “It all went by too quickly,” he said. “Football is like that, it’s always been like that for me.”

Who knows, perhaps he enjoyed himself so much that he wants to extend his career even further. “I don’t know, but if the president calls me, I’ll come back. It’s always a pleasure to play, I told him: ‘when he needs me, I’m there’.”

Mandorlini was effusive too. “We’re here and we’re truly proud to have been the architects of this match you played in,” he told the Brazilian. “So, if you want to play another one, that’s fine.”

Who knows what the future holds? For now, Ravenna fans will always have this: a day when a true legend connected people from around the world and allowed them, for one afternoon, to dream.

#870. Pochettino: I’d tell Guardiola to ‘take it’ if he’s offered US coaching job

As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America

Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.

So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.

“You know what I noticed?” Pochettino asked, smiling as he recounted the story during a meeting with reporters on Monday. “[Guardiola had a] good relationship with JT.”

Back then, Pochettino didn’t seem to be going anywhere. Only a month earlier, he’d signed a four-year contract to guide the US through the 2030 World Cup. Guardiola was, and still is, in the middle of a year-long sabbatical from coaching. He remains the federation’s white whale, often mentioned in the same breath as the US job over the past decade-plus but just as quickly dismissed as a pipe dream.

Just three months after taking in that game at Yankee Stadium, Pochettino is on his way to Manchester United and Guardiola has once again found himself at the center of the rumor mill, with reports suggesting that he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks.

On Monday, Pochettino was asked what he’d tell the Barcelona and Manchester City legend if he was asked for his opinion on the US job.

“Take it,” Pochettino said, flatly. “Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation. Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”

Guardiola was one of many topics the Argentinian manager covered during the roundtable, which lasted about an hour. At times defiant, at times emotional and cycling through Spanish and English, Pochettino spoke of his potential legacy at US Soccer, what lies ahead for him at United and how he views soccer in America as a whole.

Quotes have been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

However you assess his results, one of the inarguable successes of the Pochettino era are the relatively unheralded players whose status has risen over his tenure. The Argentine cited defender Alex Freeman and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter as two such examples, both of whom were playing in MLS when making their national team debuts under Pochettino and both now playing in Europe. Asked how he assesses players to add to the national team, and how he compares players across different leagues and playing styles, Pochettino insisted that the level of competition matters less than individual form.

“You need to project the individual player,” Pochettino said. “Because he’s playing well, the level is no issue. That player can be good, like Freeman, like Sebastian. That is the example, and I think that is so important. There is talent everywhere … This one is one of the things that we learn – all [of us], we were young and then we start to be a coach, no? That we cannot make a mistake [and] measure the level of the player because of the level of the league.”

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

With the US being his first international job, there were some doubts going in about how Pochettino would adapt to coaching without daily contact with his players and staff.

“I am ready [to return]. This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here,” Pochettino said. “Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’ [He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool]. But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good. But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything … this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”

But what did Pochettino think of his maiden international job?

“I like and not like,” he said. “I like because it provides you the possibility to manage your time, to be busy, but at the same time, be free and to have some time with your family. Now, I have a grandchild, and [number] two is coming. You can share the life with your people. But now, ciao, because now is [gestures] tra-tra-tra-tra-tra. It’s impossible to spend time with the people you want.”

In the grand scheme of international football, the US national team coaching job has never been close to the top of the list of most desirable destinations. Pochettino’s hire was seen as a possible sign that could be changing. Now, after nearly two years in the position, Pochettino believes it has.

“The vision from Europe, I promise it is completely different after the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “Now, being head coach of the USA is more prestigious. If Manchester United, or Real Madrid, or Barcelona is coming for the US coach, if you start to think about that, if you are another coach – maybe [Antonio] Conte, someone else, you say ‘oh, this is a great opportunity.’ [In my case], ‘Oh, Pochettino, from Chelsea he goes to the US? And now to Manchester United.’

Pochettino has coached some of the most famous players and clubs in the world, giving him a unique perspective on how soccer has developed in the US. Pochettino stopped short of prescribing neat solutions to improve the sport, though.

“I think that business [and] the sport, is [done] in a holistic way. Everything is important, and you cannot pick one. You cannot change one [thing], and that can change everything,” he said. “I think it’s a little bit of everything that you need to change. If you adjust this, you need to adjust this. The balance of the thing changes if you touch here, that will force you to touch all the areas in soccer here, or in the world To find the good balance, no? A process of little by little, is all that we made in these last two years. I think it’s the beginning of [a process]. If that has continuity, it’s the beginning of the new soccer in the USA that can be.

“I think that is, for me, the beginning of the change for the future: that idea that the American player can be very good, can be very competitive. The talent is here; it’s so powerful in this country. I think that is why I feel proud. Maybe that was our job, because I don’t believe in coincidence. That has happened because something needed to happen. Now the tough job is done. Maybe now [the United job] is my reward because of this tough job.”

#869. Lily Tomlin and George Schlatter Detail the Chemistry Behind Laugh-In

Lily Tomlin and Laugh-In creator George Schlatter reflected on their incredible years working on the sketch series ahead of the new documentary Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter.

You bet your sweet blippy Lily Tomlin and George Schlatter have only the best memories of Laugh-In.

The two comedy icons gave behind-the-scenes details of the very eenteresting time they shared on the sketch comedy series—which ran for six seasons from 1968 to 1973—ahead of the release of the documentary Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter, which will be available to rent or buy on all digital platforms beginning Dec. 8.

“A major, major reason for our success was that Miss Tomlin,” Schlatter exclusively shared with E! News’ Will Marfuggi. “God love her.”

And Tomlin—who joined Laugh-In halfway through season three and was a regular performer until the show ended—was forever grateful that the flying fickle finger of fate led her to Schlatter.

“When I walked into the room, he just threw his arms around me,” the 87-year-old told E! of her audition. “We’d never met. He said, ‘About time you got here, kid,’ or something like that. And he just made me feel so comfortable. I knew he got me. I knew he got me from the start.”

The moment is one that Schlatter himself also fondly remembered.

“You just walked in the room and the room lit up,” the 96-year-old shared. “The room just elevated into another space where it stayed, and Lily became a major, major part of my life, my career, and my everything.”

Tomlin—whose famous characters included the obnoxious telephone operator Ernestine—was just one of the stars to come out of Laugh-In, which was hosted by comedians Dan Rowan and Dick Martin and helped launch the careers of Goldie Hawn, Ruth Buzzi and more.

Looking back on it now, Schlatter is amazed by all the comedy they created for NBC in beautiful downtown Burbank—all of which is touched on in the new documentary that includes interviews with Tomlin, Hawn, Tom Hanks, Billy Crystal, Martin Short and more.

“We came into a time period where there was nothing,” he mused. “They were getting no rating at all. And so we could arrive and I said, ‘I’ll give you a show ’til you get a real show ready.’”

And when it comes to his memories of the award-winning series, finding Tomlin and still being able to give her a ringy-dingy all these years later is certainly one of his greatest achievements.

“There was no other Lily Tomlin,” Schlatter said. “Lily Tomlin was just a magical, magical personality that just happened and exploded. Timing was right for her, and it sure was right for me. Lily, we had a good time.”

Of course, Tomlin agreed with one of her oldest friends, adding, “It's not enough to say we had a good time because it would open the door for me on everything.”

Sock It to Me: The Legend of George Schlatter will be available for purchase or rental on all digital platforms starting Dec. 8.

For a look at more of Hollywood’s most enduring friendships, keep reading.

Nicole, a longtime fan of her sister-in-law's movies, several years ago took the opportunity to ask her to re-enact a few of her favorite movie scenes, including one from My Best Friend's Wedding.

"We were in Chicago and I said to her, 'Cameron, I need you to give it to me. I need you to get behind the luggage cart and run towards me, towards the airport,'" she said on the Everything Iconic with Danny Pellegrino podcast in May 2024. "I really think like at a certain point, we were driving past things and I was like, 'Say this. Say this. Say this.' And she really just let me have it. It was very generous of her."

Thank goodness Lawrence is down to hang or we might have been robbed of one of our most beloved set of besties. Their friendship was born from an email the Oscar winner sent after watching Schumer's 2015 comedy. "I emailed her after I saw Trainwreck and said, 'I don't know where to get started. I guess I should just say it: I'm in love with you,'" she recalled to The New York Times. "We started emailing, and then emailing turned to texting." But what really solidified their bond was Schumer's casual invite for her new pal to join her and her high school friends in the Hamptons. Shocked when she said yes, Schumer relaxed when she realized Lawrence is "the coolest chick you'll ever meet," she said on The Daily Show. "She's the best hang, she was like one of the gang."

Who doesn't want a friend that basically owns real estate in your corner? They've been tight since falling in love at first sight at the 2004 premiere of Man on Fire. "It was one of those instant chemistry things where you just feel like, 'I love this person. I love being around this person. This person makes me laugh,'" Lopez recalled to Entertainment Tonight of her Brooklyn-bred bestie. And Remini was among those getting loud in celebration of Lopez's performance at President Joe Biden's inauguration. "I wrote her and said, 'You know, you're a girl from the Bronx. 'Like, what you did today was really inspiring, and it was just beautiful to watch," she told E! News. "Just beautiful.'"

The gold standard of celebrity besties—this trio has been in lock step since their days of sharing salads on the Warner Brothers lot. "They grew up together and went through this formidable life experience that was Friends," a source told E! News. So, much like you might meet up with coworkers from your first job, they make it a point to get happy hours (and the occasional major reunion) on their calendar. "Geographically it's not hard to be at Courteney's Sunday dinners or at a pool party at Jen's house," notes the source. "They all feel incredibly close and always will be."

Making other friends jealous since a chance meeting at improv training in 1993, the frequent costars are so close, they liken their bond to that of family. "I think that Tina and I are chosen sisters," Poehler, whose sole sibling is younger brother Greg, told PopSugar while discussing their 2015 flick Sisters. "I think we are chosen family, so I think it's been fun to experience that thing I never got to experience in real life."

"It was like, you know, how people say love at first sight? We had that thing," Philipps told Entertainment Weekly of their initial interaction on the Dawson's Creek set. "We had that friend connection. It was just an immediate: 'Of course we're drinking wine and smoking cigarettes and getting in bar fights.' We just had an immediate love for each other that's continued over the years." Fortunately for us, we get to voyeuristically follow along as they work red carpets, wear coordinating outfits and occasionally dye Williams' hair the most perfect shade of millennial pink.

Having had "women that were really helpful to me when I was pregnant," mom of two Washington has always strived to pay it forward with her celeb pals. "I really do try to have those conversations openly and honestly as possible, especially with my soul sister, with Eva," she told Entertainment Tonight. Her advice was well-received when Longoria welcomed son Santiago in 2018, with the Grand Hotel actress calling the Scandal alum, "basically my doula."

More than 20 years after nabbing Oscar gold, the Good Will Hunting scribes are back at it again, working on The Last Duel. And though it's been a minute since they shared a screen, their bromance hasn't wavered. "I've known him for 35 years, and we grew up together," Damon told Entertainment Tonight in 2016. "We were both in love with the same thing—acting and filmmaking. I think we fed on each other's obsession during really formative, important years and that bonded us for life."

The connection between two of television's most powerful women dates back to 1976 when they were working at a Baltimore station—though anchors (Winfrey helmed the 6 p.m. hour) and production assistants (that was King), didn't generally socialize. "The newsroom hierarchy," CBS This Morning cohost King recalled in their O Interview. But with a heavy snow coming down, Winfrey invited the $12,000-a-year PA to sleep at her house. "The next day," said Winfrey, "we went to the mall." And a friendship was born over Casual Corner sweaters.

Sure, your friend dates likely don't involve watching your pal play for Wimbledon and U.S. Open titles or get-togethers at a palace. But the bond between the tennis champ and the Duchess of Sussex began much like any other—over girl talk. "We hit it off immediately," Meghan wrote on her now-shuttered lifestyle website The Tig of their meeting at a 2014 Super Bowl event. "Taking pictures, laughing through the flag football game we were both playing in, and chatting not about tennis or acting, but about all the good old fashioned girly stuff."

Game of Thrones may have wrapped, but the relationship between the Stark sisters lives on. In fact Williams, who served as Turner's maid of honor when she wed Joe Jonas in 2019, is convinced the best thing to come of the eight-season HBO hit wasn't any of its 12 Emmy awards. "It was like one big elaborate thing to find me a best friend. This whole show!" she joked to E! News at the final season premiere. "I'm kidding. It's been incredible. To have a friend like that on something as wild as this is just like a godsend, really."

Friends gifted Aniston with more than one goals-worthy bestie. Before she and Witherspoon developed their Apple TV+ series, The Morning Show, they portrayed sisters on the NBC hit. "I was 23 years old and had just had a baby," the Oscar winner recalled to Harper's Bazaar of her two-episode arc back in 2000. "I was nursing Ava [Phillippe] on set, and Jen just kept going, 'You have a baby?' I was like, 'I know, it's weird.' And I remember her being like, 'Where are you going?' And I was like, 'I'm pumping!'" Though Witherspoon felt admittedly nervous, she said Aniston couldn't have been more sweet: "We've been friends ever since."

Equal parts intriguing and covetable, this pairing was solidified at The Comedy Central Roast of Justin Bieber in 2015 before they teamed up for their VH1 cooking show, Martha & Snoop's Potluck Dinner Party. "She different, ya know, than what I'm accustomed," the marijuana-loving 17-time Grammy winner told LA Weekly of the Westchester-based domestic doyenne. "But then again she's so what I'm accustomed to. 'Cause she people. She just look different and she was born in a different era, but if you hang out with her and chill with her, she just like anybody else. That's why it works, because she never says nothing that's crazy in my ears. It's always like, 'Damn, I thought you would say that. OK.' That's why we get down, that's why we connected, Martha. 'Cause it feels like holy matrimony, and not holy macaroni."

Theirs is a newer alliance, but no less desirable. After years of existing in the same orbit, the "Hotline Bling" rapper and the "Hello" songstress, who have over a dozen Grammys between them, began throwing out the idea of a collaboration. "I really want us to do an official remix," she told Canada's etalk of their well-coordinated hits. "I love Drake. I love Drake so much. I even got the coat that's in the video, I got it delivered the other day, I ordered it. The red one." He responded by saying, "I'd do anything with Adele. I'd literally go to Adele's house right now and do laundry for her." Instead, they grabbed a bite to eat and hit up an L.A. bowling alley. Next time, you know, call us on our cell phone.

#867. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

#866. How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace

Crystal Palace are Thomas Frank's third London club after previous spells with Brentford and Tottenham

"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.

The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.

Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.

"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".

But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.

"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.

"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.

Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Would Thomas Frank be a good fit for Crystal Palace?

Frank, who places a major emphasis on set-piece organisation, will have to hit the ground running at Palace, who have lost their past four league games.

They have conceded more goals than anyone else in the Premier League (24) and have scored only 10 themselves.

"If you want someone to go in and restore some stability and defensive solidity while improving the set-piece element of the team, then Thomas Frank is the perfect man for the job," Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.

With the Premier League season just 10 games old, Frank certainly has time to turn it around and will have targets in mind when the transfer window opens in January.

Palace sold France centre-back Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea for Â£52m and Colombia right-back Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest for Â£22m during the summer transfer window.

Allnutt added: "We know they have sold so many good players and so far I don't think they have really replaced them adequately."

Another challenge for Frank is getting midfielder Adam Wharton, who has not played for England since March, back to something like his best form.

These are all challenges the new manager will relish.

After his bruising experience at Tottenham - having established Brentford in the Premier League - Frank has decided to climb back on the hamster wheel with Palace.

"Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.

Crystal Palace fan calls Thomas Frank 'the perfect hire'

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

There is also one significant factor in Frank's favour. Although Palace may be bottom of the Premier League, they are certainly not cut adrift as they sit just two points from safety.

The side propping up the table at this stage have had an average of just three points in the past 10 seasons, but for as bad as they've been, Palace have seven - the most the bottom side have had after 10 games for 24 years.

#865. ‘We want to win it’: Tuchel says Nations League can set up England for Euro 2028 glory

Winning Nations League ‘the best preparation’ for Euros

England to be seeded in Friday’s draw after Spain win

Thomas Tuchel believes winning the Nations League would provide England with the springboard to Euro 2028 glory. The head coach watched his team close out the calendar year with a sensational 3-2 victory against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium on ­Sunday.

It meant England leapfrogged the world champions to finish top of their Nations League group and ensured seeded status for the ­quarter-final draw on Friday. England will co‑host the European Championship and Tuchel wants to go into it as the Nations League winners.

“It is for me and for us,” he said when asked about the importance of the Nations League and its potential to help a team to bigger and better things. “I saw and heard about the celebrations in Portugal when they won it last year [beating Spain on penalties in the final]. It is just the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We don’t think so far, but it’s a fact.

“We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves, to gain in confidence and to see where we are … to adjust our game where we need a bit of adjustment. That’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it. But first of all, we need to win the quarter-final.”

The defender Ezri Konsa echoed Tuchel’s thoughts. “The Nations League is a trophy and silverware going into the Euros would be ­massive for us,” he said. “We want to win the Euros and we know it is on home soil. That will give us a ­massive boost.”

England surged into a 3-0 lead against Spain only to have Elliot Anderson sent off in the 63rd minute when he conceded a penalty. Mikel Oyarzabal scored it and the closing stages were nervy for England. There were shades of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentinaas England sought desperately to defend their advantage.

“Playing with 10 men against the world champions would be difficult,” Konsa said. “The amount of balls coming into the box we dealt with really well.

“The World Cup has gone. We have passed that. We are focused on winning each game and we know we have the Euros coming up.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate.

Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals.

The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance.

Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association

“It’s very important to end the year on a high. You end it with huge confidence going into next year’s set of games. We are taking it camp by camp. But going into March [and the Nations League quarter-finals] we will have a lot of confidence.”

Tuchel said: “We took the next steps after the World Cup and I’m very proud of the performance against Spain. It’s a real statement victory. It was the way we won; the way we played the third phase was very impressive. You could see the steps we take between every single match.”

#864. Charli XCX Has Fierce Response to John Summit’s Grammys 2027 Criticism

Charli XCX, who won Best Dance/Electronic Album at the 2025 Grammys for Brat, responded to DJ John Summit’s criticism that the 2027 nominees in the Dance/Electronic categories were a “f--king joke.”

Charli XCX is ready to boom clap back at some criticism.

After American DJ John Summit clarified he wasn’t dissing the 2027 Grammy nominees when he said the nominations were a “f--king joke” for not respecting “real” electronic dance music, the Brat singer proved she did not love it.

As Charli wrote on X Nov. 16 in response, “Not this guy again!”

Summit (real name John Schuster) has previously praised Charli’s music on social media, even requesting to collaborate with her. However, he wrote on X in 2024, “Charli has left me on read but that’s ok i still stan.”

While Summit has never been nominated for a Grammy, the “Girl so confusing” singer won two trophies in the Dance/Electronic Music categories in 2025, including for Best Dance/Electronic Album for Brat. (She also won the 2025 Grammy for Best Recording Package.)

This year, Charli earned three nominations—one for Best Alternative Music Album for her album Music, Fashion, Film and two for Visual Media for her work on the Margot Robbie film Wuthering Heights.

After Summit was shut out of this year’s nominations—which saw artists like Madonna, Tinashe, Fred Again.., and Slayyyter among the Dance/Electronic nominees—he shared his frustration on social media.

“Never submitting to the grammys again unless s--t changes,” he wrote in part on X. “The whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars.”

Amid the backlash to his criticism, the “Where You Are” artist walked back his ire.

“Logging back on as i realized i didn’t do a good job of making my point earlier,” he wrote in a separate post to X. “My intent was not to drag other artists down and i seriously congratulate everyone who was nominated. They fully deserve the recognition.”

Still, Summit added, “I just think there should be an extra category for more dance music djs & producers.”

Of course, Summit wasn’t the only artist left out of the 2027 Grammy nominees. For all the shocking snubs and surprises from this year’s nominations, keep reading…

Abrams failed to snag any nominations for her latest album Daughter From Hell, which she submitted for Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album. Her single "Hit the Wall" was also absent from the Song of the Year, Record of the Year and Best Pop Solo Performance lists.

Abrams has previously received two nominations for Best New Artist in 2024 and Best Pop Duo Performance for "Us" which featured Taylor Swift in 2025.

While Grande picked up some surprise nominations for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance for "For Good" alongside Cynthia Erivo, as well as Song of the Year and Best Music Video for "hate that I made you love me," and Best Pop Vocal Album for Petal, she was snubbed for Album of the Year.

Although Kahan scored one nomination for Best Contemporary Folk Album, he was not included in the major categories like Album of the Year and Song of the Year for his hit The Great Divide.

Beyoncé is famously the most decorated Grammy-winning artist—the 35-time winner scored her 100th nomination this year— but her Best R&B Solo Performance nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" was somewhat of a surprise considering its delayed release in celebration of B'Day's 20th anniversary in July.

This year was big for Hobert, who released her debut album Who's the Clown last year, but she failed to score a nod for Best New Artist. (Her brother Malcolm Todd was also left off the shortlist.)

That's actually not all for this much-anticipated sequel. The Devil Wears Prada 2 scored a surprise nomination for Best Compilation Soundtrack For Visual Media alongside Stranger Things season five, Wicked: For Good, The Wizard of Oz at the Sphere and Wuthering Heights.

It's been a long time coming for the first-time Grammy nominee, who scored her first nods for Best Dance/Electronic Recording for "Melatonin" as well as Best Dance Pop Recording for "Too Easy."

Swift wasn't totally snubbed by the Recording Academy—she earned nods for Record of the Year, Album of the Year, Song of the Year, Best Pop Duo Performance alongside Sabrina Carpenter, Best Song Written for a Visual Media and more. But The Life of a Showgirl was not among Best Pop Vocal Album contenders, while "I Knew It, I Knew You" was snubbed for Best Country Song and Best Country Solo Performance.

Still, it was a surprise to see "I Knew It, I Knew You" score a nomination for Song of the Year, a category introduced by Swift herself during the nomination livestream, given Swift's other hits from The Life of a Showgirl.

The hype hasn't died down, Wicked is still oh so very popular. Wicked: For Good scored two nominations including Best Song Written For Visual Media and Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance.

Disco All The Time, Grammy Occasionally. The "Aperture" singer failed to score recognition for his latest album in any category. Styles has three Grammy wins under his belt, including Album of the Year for Harry's House in 2023.

Her comeback is far from over. The pop star received her first Grammy nominations in 16 years, racking up nods for Best Dance Pop Recording, Best Dance/Electronic Recording, Best Dance/Electronic Album and Best Pop Duo/Group Performance for "Bring Your Love" alongside Carpenter.

Although Lefty rose to massive acclaim this year for hits like "Boston," she failed to receive any recognition by The Recording Academy.

Following a two-year hiatus, West scored a nod for Best Rap Album for Bully.

#863. India's Dhoni retires from playing role with Chennai Super Kings

Nicknamed "Captain Cool," MS Dhoni led India to World Cup titles in 20 and 50-over ‌one-day formats; 45-year-old retires from playing role with Indian Premier League's Chennai Super Kings; will become 'team mentor' from 2027 season; Dhoni retired from international cricket in 2020

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former India captain MS Dhoni has retired from playing with Chennai Super Kings in the Indian Premier League and will take up a new role as team mentor from the 2027 season.

Dhoni was bought by the Super Kings in the inaugural IPL auction in 2008 and went on to guide the franchise to five IPL championships.

The 45-year-old spent 17 out of 19 seasons with the Super Kings, also playing for Rising Pune Supergiant when the Chennai club were suspended. Dhoni finishes his IPL career with 5,439 runs and an average of 38.30 across 278 matches.

"There is no CSK without MS Dhoni," Super Kings owner N Srinivasan said on the club's website. "For nearly two decades, we have walked and grown alongside each other, through triumphs, setbacks and everything in between.

"Dhoni will always be a part of our identity. This will always be his home."

Dhoni, who hails from Ranchi, enjoys huge popularity in the southern Indian city of Chennai where ‌crowds throng stadia just to get a glimpse of their "Thala", the Tamil word for leader.

Runs stopped flowing from his blade in recent years ‌but legions of his fans still filled the stands to watch Dhoni batting lower down the order.

Even that was not possible this year, however, and Dhoni sat out the entire season with a calf strain, which effectively ⁠signalled the end of his career.

Dhoni has been the ​face of the franchise since joining them in ​2008 and played two seasons with Rising Pune Super Giant ​only when Chennai were handed a two-year suspension following a corruption ⁠scandal.

"While we will miss seeing him in yellow on the field, we are glad that he will keep guiding our players," Chennai managing director KS ⁠Viswanathan said.

"The bond will continue to grow ​and shape this team for years to come."

Nicknamed "Captain Cool" for ​his astute leadership and unflappable temperament, Dhoni led India to World Cup titles in the 20 and 50-over ‌one-day formats.

#861. Swansea braced to lose Vítor Matos as Strasbourg seek to replace Hugo Oliveira

Matos has indicated a desire for move to Ligue 1

Championship club would be due compensation

Swansea City are increasingly resigned to their head coach, Vítor Matos, joining Strasbourg after he indicated a desire to join Chelsea’s sister club. The Ligue 1 club have approached Swansea with a view to Matos succeeding Hugo Oliveira.

Strasbourg, acquired by Chelsea’s parent company BlueCo in 2023, have identified Matos as a replacement for Oliveira, who has won three of 10 league matches since succeeding Gary O’Neil in July. The French club are hovering two points above the relegation zone.

Matos is under contract until 2030 and Swansea would be due significant compensation for the 38-year-old, a former Liverpool academy and development team coach.

Matos has won admirers since taking charge of Swansea last November and, despite one win in their past five games, has the south Wales club in the Championship playoff spots. Swansea finished last season in 11th and backed Matos in the transfer market this summer in the hope of pushing on.

Swansea’s next match is at home to West Brom on Saturday, before a trip to Middlesbrough and a south Wales derby against Cardiff in the Welsh capital.

Matos, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea this month, joined the club from Marítimo, a Portuguese second-division club. His 12-game spell in charge of Maritimo represented his first senior management job.

Strasbourg and Chelsea share a close relationship and have traded players, with Emmanuel Emegha and Valentín Barco joining the English club in recent months.

In the most notable move between the clubs, however, Liam Rosenior left his role as Strasbourg head coach to take charge of Chelsea in January, but the former Hull manager was sacked in April. O’Neil succeeded Rosenior but joined Ipswich in June.
