#814. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers are revealed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said, "I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he had the credibility and unifying potential to be able to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer", he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different when the heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered some setbacks.

Uefa called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, and then potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

Could Infantino even be ruled ineligible to stand? According to Portuguese lawyer Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - Infantino should not be allowed to be a candidate in the election as Fifa rules limit presidents to three terms. In 2022, Fifa's Council agreed that his first period in office - between 2016 and 2019 - should not count as he was effectively completing the remainder of Blatter's term after his resignation. But as Maduro has said, a national association or confederation would need to challenge this decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

Japan Football Association honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand, along with former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega. But with uncertainty over how much support either man will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#813. Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling

Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France

There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling.

Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal’s under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records.

In scoring his first under-21s goal, in the penultimate minute of regular time, Dowman eclipsed Jude Bellingham to become the team’s youngest scorer at 16 years and 320 days, three days after surpassing the Real Madrid midfielder’s record as the under-21s’ youngest player. Bellingham was almost four months older than Dowman when he scored his first goal for the age group, in September 2020. Bellingham made only four appearances for the under-21s, a result of being fast-tracked into the senior team, and Dowman could emulate him again, though he is expected to feature in next summer’s Under-21 European Championship in Albania and Serbia.

The common view from coaches and teammates, and something stressed by Lee Carsley, the under-21s head coach, is that it is easy to forget Dowman is a month shy of his 17th birthday. Against France, it was also extremely easy to overlook that this was Dowman’s first start for the under-21s, after a substitute appearance against Portugal last Friday. His first action set the tone on Monday, using his body to box off the ball then jinking up the right flank, zipping it through the legs of Dayann Methalie before skating forward and sending the Sunderland left-back juddering on to his backside.

Dowman exhibited plenty of neat touches, a couple of effortless first-time passes, but those who have watched him develop say his work rate and willingness to do the other side of the game is one of his biggest strengths. “We look at Max and see how good he is on the ball, how attacking he is, but I thought he was outstanding off the ball,” Carsley said, presumably thinking of the moment Dowman scampered deep into his own half to intercept a stray France pass. He was not finished after scoring either. At one point he had five blue shirts haring after him as he stormed into the France half and, seconds later, his quick feet lured opposition captain, Nathan Zézé, into a foul on the edge of the box.

Dowman is among the next wave of players pushing to step up to Thomas Tuchel’s squad, perhaps at its forefront. It is a well-trodden path and the current crop need not look too far for inspiration. Elliot Anderson and Jarell Quansah, both of whom started England’s triumph at the last under-21 Euros in Bratislava, began Sunday’s memorable victory for the seniors in Madrid. Jobe Bellingham and Josh King are the latest players to make the transition into Tuchel’s squad and more will follow.

Jack Hinshelwood and Trey Nyoni, of Brighton and Liverpool respectively, impressed at the base of midfield and the 19-year-old Mikey Moore, another to score on his first start for the under-21s, shone down the left flank, opening the scoring. The Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong entered as a substitute and supplied Dowman’s winner, and Armstrong’s clubmate Tyrique George also showed promise after replacing Moore. Archie Gray captained the under-21s against Portugal but did not feature on Monday, with Carsley revealing he has spoken to the Tottenham midfielder about Scotland wanting him to switch allegiance. “I just said to him: ‘Keep me in the picture, if it’s something that you were thinking of,’” Carsley said. “I think Archie is very connected to our pathway.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

England’s budding talent is not confined to the under-21s. Carsley took a closer look at Brian Madjo, the imposing 17-year-old striker who scored on his Aston Villa debut in the Super Cup in August, the Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven and the West Brom forward Jimmy-Jay Morgan, who signed from Chelsea in the summer, before his squad departed for Bristol last week, the trio joining the under-21s for four days of training at St George’s Park.

Dowman, after two under-21 appearances comprising a total of a little more than 120 minutes, is putting the squeeze on. “Max is doing something special for his age and he is pushing people a lot older than him,” said Moore, who is on loan from Tottenham at Köln and hopes to face his idol Harry Kane and Bayern Munich on Friday. “He’s a top kid. You kind of forget how old he is. My little brother is 17 and he [Dowman] feels older to me than my little brother … He has been top and everywhere he goes, he just takes that next step.”

#812. London City's Goodwin gets first England call-up

Izzy Goodwin has scored three goals in five WSL appearances for London City

London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.

The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal.

"We have always seen her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending.

"She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."

There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.

Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.

The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup.

"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman.

"We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job.

"Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."

Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.

England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break.

"The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman.

"We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."

Sarina Wiegman led England to victory at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025

Wiegman was speaking to media at St George's Park for the first time since signing a new contract that will run until the end of Euro 2029.

It means she could oversee England's fortunes at next year's World Cup if they beat Ukraine, as well as heading up a Team GB squad at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Asked why she wanted to extend her stay, Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Well, first of all the FA is happy with me and I'm really happy with them.

"I'm really grateful for that environment. That is one [reason]. Secondly, I still feel a great connection with staff and players, and of course the country!

"Then we have the challenges ahead. The major tournaments always motivate me. You don't get many moments with the team because it's not like it is at a club.

"In a tournament, you have those moments where you are really together, you can get somewhere with the group and that really excites me.

"Yes, the Olympics would be really great. Next year it's the World Cup, then it's the Olympics, then it's the Euros â that journey ahead really excites me."

Wiegman's contract renewal was kept under wraps and it came as a surprise following their two-legged victory over Greece in October.

The Dutchwoman, who has guided England to successive European titles, said conversations had been ongoing for a while but she had not planned ahead.

"When I signed that first contract in 2020 to join in 2021, it was a four-year contract and I thought, 'ok, this is a long contract, it would be really great if things go well'.

"We all got so excited so I signed another contract until 2027 and now I have until 2029. That is eight years. I never expected that. I also never planned so far ahead.

"I want to feel that I can contribute to the environment and the development of things. I also want that from the other party. You want it to fit and for it to work.

"That decision came over time. At one point you think: 'Yeah, I'm getting really excited again.' That is what you want. To feel the energy, to feel the excitement.

"I still think we have things we can improve. We know the game is improving so quickly so we have to adapt all the time. When you stand still, you are lost."

Wiegman is also determined to improve as a coach and has enjoyed overseeing the development of younger talent as the Lionesses transition.

"It starts with me and about how I am going to develop. I keep learning things about myself too. You need to know yourself really well to do this job," she added.

"The staff and the players will always challenge me in the right ways. It goes back and forth. That is what I want. I really want to improve myself all the time."

#811. Wiegman cites young talent as key to new England deal after calling up Goodwin

Head coach excited by ‘high potential’ of players

Striker Goodwin and keeper Cox in squad for first time

Sarina Wiegman says the potential in England’s emerging young players helped convince her to extend her contract until the end of 2029’s European Championship.

The Lionesses head coach, whose previous deal was due to expire next year, gave first senior call-ups to the striker Isobel Goodwin and goalkeeper Katie Cox on Tuesday as she named her squad for December’s two-leg World Cup qualifying playoff against Ukraine.

Speaking to the media for the first time since signed her new contract in October, Wiegman described the Football Association as “a trailblazer with the women’s game and a great federation to work for” and said: “I’m really happy with the team but also talents coming through, which is exciting, and there’s now some high potential, and hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players, if not already. And I hope to have a part in that, too, and have a contribution to that. While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited.

“The majority of their development is happening [at their clubs] but when they come to our environment, I hope to have a little part of that contribution.”

The Dutchwoman has led England to three consecutive major tournament finals, lifting two European titles, since taking charge in 2021 on a deal to 2025. Asked whether she had expected that to become an eight-year stay, she said: “No. I thought: ‘Four years, that’s a long time.’ Then it became six years and that looks like it’s becoming eight years. I would never have expected all of the things that we have reached.”

Will she call it a day in 2029? “Well, I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know! I don’t plan that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”

Goalkeepers: Katie Cox (Nottingham Forest on loan from Chelsea), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool)Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Taylor Hinds (Arsenal), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Poppy Pattinson (London City Lionesses), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Grace Clinton (Manchester City), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Ella Toone (Manchester United), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)Forwards: Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea), Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Isobel Goodwin (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal)

Wiegman, whose latest 25-player squad includes 10 players with fewer than 10 caps, watched from the stands at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday as Goodwin scored for London City Lionesses with a terrific finish against Arsenal. She said of the 23-year-old: “We always knew she’s a huge talent [with] a high potential. We’re watching a lot of games over periods of time, all the time, so we [had] kept an eye on her anyway, but I think it also helped that she had that great goal and a great performance last Sunday.

“She has some different qualities. She’s really fast too. She can head – she showed that also in attacking set plays and defending set plays also – and she can score goals. Does she need to step up to the next level? Absolutely. But you can tell that she’s improving.”

Wiegman was unable to call upon several injured players, including Lauren James and Alex Greenwood. She included Manchester United’s Ella Toone, who was initially left out of September’s squad before being recalled for the playoff against Greece. Wiegman said of Toone: “She has impressed us really well. She responded really well. And going back to [her] club, she’s done well too. And that’s what has been fed back to me too.”

Cox is rare in getting an England call-up while playing in the second-tier WSL2. The 20-year-old is on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea.

The Lionesses face Ukraine on neutral territory in Spain in the away leg on 1 December before playing them at Wembley four days later.

#810. Golden Bachelor’s Peg Munson Reveals Reason for Mel Owens Breakup

After Peg Munson and Mel Owens—who met and fell in love on season two of The Golden Bachelor—called it quits, she’s sharing insight into what led to their split.

Peg Munson is sharing the thornier parts of her and Mel Owens' love story.

Nearly one month after announcing she and the former NFL player had decided to break up, the retired firefighter reflected on what led to the couple's flame going out.

“We came to the understanding because it wasn’t about marriage for us,” Munson noted during the Nov. 16 episode on the She’s All Bach podcast. “He didn’t want to get married. I didn’t want to get married. We didn’t want to be engaged. We’re in our 60s. That’s great for the young kids, but when you’re in your 60s, it’s like, ‘Look, I just need to know if you’re dateable.’”

Noting that she's experienced a "rough couple of months," Munson shared the turning point came a few weeks before she shared their breakup publicly.

“I always have said relationships don’t create things; they reveal things,” she added. “First six months were great. I felt like I was a main character in a fantasy romance novel, and it was wonderful. But then real life kicked in.”

However, as Munson noted, she “noticed some things" and "wasn’t okay with it."

“I would try to talk to him, communicate with him," she explained. "And as everybody saw on the show, I mean, he is just not a lot of emotion at all.”

But ultimately, when Munson got sick and Owens didn't check in, she realized that their issues stemmed from a deeper place. "I was like, ‘Alright, well,'" she explained, "'is this guy capable of meeting me where I’m at?’”

“He was pretty hurt because he didn’t see it coming,” she added. “It wasn’t mutual. I tried to talk to him about some of the things that I needed, and he just wasn’t responsive.”

In late October, Munson detailed the decision to call it quits, with their breakup coming one year after the finale. (Though Owens presented a ring, he didn't propose—but assured her they would remain together.)

"As a lot of you guys know I went on the Golden Bachelor, hoping to find love, and I did," she shared in an Oct. 21 Instagram video. "And you know, for that I'm grateful.”

“I did have to make the difficult decision to step away from the relationship,” Munson noted at thet time. “Sometimes, even when there's love, it just doesn't turn out the way that we hoped. So right now, I'm just, I'm just focusing on healing my heart and just focusing on myself, my health, and looking forward to the next chapter.”

Munson, 63, concluded her message by wishing Owens, 67, the best of luck.

“I'm grateful for the memories," she continued, "and most of all, I'm grateful for you guys along this journey with me.”

For a look at where more Bachelor Nation couples stand today, keep reading...

Even before Mel Owen's season of The Golden Bachelor kicked off, he was hit with a few penalties after going on the MGoBlue Podcasts With Jon Jansen and insisting, "if they’re 60 or over, I’m cutting them," adding that he wanted them to "try to stay away from the artificial hips and the wigs."

And while Peg Munson is a fellow sexagenarian, his connection with the retired firefighter and bomb tech was quite explosive, with the former NFL linebacker praising her as "high-energy" to Glamour.

Though he didn't take a knee during his November 2025 finale, the sports lawyer still offered up a Neil Lane sparkler, saying, "This represents our commitment to love, to give us time to figure out together what our future holds."

Munson announced in October 2026 that the couple had split, sharing on Instagram, "I did have to make the difficult decision to step away from the relationship. Sometimes, even when there's love, it just doesn't turn out the way that we hoped. Posting a snippet of himself and Jess Edwards (she took a swing at Bachelor Joey Graziadei's heart) revealing that they were falling for one another—Bachelor code for I'm not quite ready to say, "I love you"—he wrote on his Instagram Stories in August 2025 that he'd "already won."

Hard same from Jess, who wrote on her main feed, "just feeling a lil giddy about this man & whatnot."

And they were certainly smiling when, after choosing their relationship over the $250,000 prize, they got engaged and walked away with a surprise check worth $190,000.

Since then, their love led her to Dallas, Jess revealing during Mel's November 2025 After the Finale Rose special that she was Texas-bound in a few weeks.

#809. Blackburn boss Mowbray steps back over health issues

Tony Mowbray's last game in charge of Blackburn Rovers was an impressive 2-1 win over West Ham United before November's international break

Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.

The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.

Mowbray had previously taken time out of the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

Rovers said Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds would take responsibility for first-team duties "for the time being".

BBC Sport was initially told Mowbray had "stepped down" but we have since been updated that he has "stepped back". No further details have been given although the club are not thought to be looking for a successor.

"Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers," Mowbray said in a statement., external

"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.

"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.

"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."

Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after a they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.

They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.

The announcement comes before Sunday's Lancashire derby against Burnley at Turf Moor, which was set to be Mowbray's 900th game in management as well as his 63rd birthday.

Mowbray has been in management for over two decades and his first spell at Blackburn ended at the conclusion of the 2021-22 season when he was eventually replaced by Jon Dahl Tomasson.

He subsequently held roles with Sunderland, Birmingham and a second spell with West Bromwich Albion before his return to Ewood Park.

In his first spell at Blackburn, he could not halt the club's relegation from the Championship, yet he led them to promotion back from League One at the first attempt and subsequently re-established them in the second tier.

In February 2024, he had been diagnosed with cancer but was eventually given the all-clear following treatment.

He leaves with Blackburn in better shape than they were during a tumultuous 2025-26 campaign, which finished with Michael O'Neill opting not to take the manager's job on a full-time basis and instead choosing to remain as boss of Northern Ireland.

"Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much," Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood added.

"Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can."

#808. Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes

A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation

“Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes.

The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

“There are two types of humans,” Jorge Valdano narrates, “Carlos Bilardo and everyone else.” Ricardo “El Gringo” Giusti recounts how he buried a sweet in the pitch before kick-off of every game, just one of the many cábalas the Argentina squad religiously followed under pressure from their obsessive manager. On the eve of the match with England, the players requested lighter shirts as the official ones were too heavy when drenched in sweat. Footage of women working at the squad hotel hand-stitching the numbers on to light T-shirts bought locally, shot by the players themselves with a handheld camera, conveys an intimacy in stark contrast to grainy archive material depicting British explorers in the South Atlantic.

Rather than run-of-the-mill talking head-style interviews with members of both teams, the interviewees are shot in monochrome, widescreen closeups, “like Roman statues”, as Cabral told the Guardian. Like monuments to themselves, the camera lingers on their eyes. What are they watching? We don’t know if they see what we see, if they are reliving the match, or seeing a cut of the actual film.

The documentary pivots around Diego Maradona’s two goals. I have long ceased to think of them as two separate goals. They are a single event, a handful of minutes when everything that is possible in football happened before our very eyes: the ugly, rule-breaking handball followed by the spectacular, beautiful gambeta. The film cleverly uses a sequence of stills taken by the Mexican photographer Alejandro Ojeda Carbajal to prove the handball, with a tongue-in-cheek nod to the paradox that they have been credited and licensed through the Englishman Bob Thomas ever since.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Films about football are hard to get right because football is a narrative form in itself. This one comes pretty close to being as good as it gets. Slick and elegant, if at times a little too glossy, The Match is an excellent piece of work filled with beautiful images, such as the crisp vintage radio illustrating soldiers listening to the game in the trenches. There are also newsreels of Margaret Thatcher and Argentinian generals at the height of the Falklands/Malvinas conflict; a score that includes Queen and giants of Argentinian rock such as Charly García. Nostalgia, history, and the backdrop of the war, handled with respect and sensitivity.

The perversity of Argentina’s military is reflected in images of an emaciated soldier spliced to the voice of a general who dismisses claims the troops were cold and starving: “They probably eat better than they did at home.” Lou Armour, a British veteran, explains he couldn’t see young Argentinians as the enemy. “We both suffered a tragedy,” Cabral says. “I’m interested in the human duality in which we go from killing each other to hugging each other.” Cabral asks when a match starts and when it ends, and also when a conflict does so.

Valdano reads Juan López y John Ward, a Jorge Luis Borges poem about the war, in Spanish. Lineker, sitting by his side, utters “very moving”, also in Spanish. English and Spanish coexist throughout the film, including in the scene showing a table football game in which John Barnes and Peter Shilton take on against Giusti, Óscar Ruggeri and Jorge Burruchaga. Burruchaga, the scorer of the winning goal in the 1986 World Cup final, cheers his opponent: “Vamos, Peter!”

An audience containing young people reacted to the documentary with a standing ovation at the London screening, where Shilton was the only cast member present. In Buenos Aires, the release of the documentary, which coincided with this summer’s World Cup, saw cinemas packed with young people. For a generation in England and Argentina who never saw the 1986 classic, almost everything in The Match is new.

The Match is in UK cinemas from 20 November

#807. Vanessa Hudgens Tries New Cosmetic Procedure After Welcoming 2 Kids

Vanessa Hudgens—who shares two kids with husband Cole Tucker—chronicled her experience trying a new cosmetic procedure: "Because after two babies, the tummy ain't what it used to be.”

Vanessa Hudgens has her head in the game when it comes to a little me-time.

The High School Musical alum shared insight into the cosmetic treatment she uses to firm up her body following the births of her and husband Cole Tucker’s two kids.

“So, I finally got a moment away from the kiddos, and mama is treating herself with a new treatment,” Hudgens said in a Nov. 16 TikTok video. “I'm so excited! It's called Everesse. It's skin tightening my face, my neck, and my stomach. Because after two babies, the tummy ain't what it used to be.”

And while the start of something new can be daunting, Hudgens—who welcomed a son with Tucker, 30, in July 2024 and a daughter in November 2025—proved she’s always up to the challenge as she took viewers along for her first session.

“We're in the robe. Let's do this thing,” she said before showing a close-up of herself getting the treatment, which includes a wand gliding over her skin. “Like I said, no needles, no downtime.”

Plus, the 37-year-old was in and out in a tick, tick…boom!

“That was so easy and quick, and there's no redness,” she said after the treatment. “I feel like my skin is literally so much tighter. But I'm so excited because apparently, it just keeps working. The collagen keeps producing, and you keep seeing better and better results. I'm not over this. I'm freaking out. This is amazing.”

Since welcoming her little ones, The Princess Switch star has been transparent about the realities of motherhood.

"Balance? I don’t know her," she quipped to E! News in August 2025. "Life is crazy and time is a really precious thing. I am a person of extremes—I'm all in doing one thing or another. So I guess that's balance, if you call extremes balance.”

She continued, "Being a mom is literally the most exhausting thing on the entire planet."

Still, the Spring Breakers actress is cherishing every moment of her journey. As she put it, becoming a mom has taught her to "slow down and enjoy the moment."

“It's so easy to focus on things in the future,” Hudgens added. “Say, ‘I'll be happy when,’ or, ‘Things will be easier when.’ But that's not what's important. What's important is the moment that is in front of you."

But she’s not the only celeb feeling fabulous after a cosmetic procedure. Keep reading for more stars who have detailed their own experiences…

The Oscar winner admitted she “can’t really get very much done” in order to maintain "movement in my face,” but she has volunteered as tribute on some procedures.

“I get baby Botox, but I can't do a lot,” she told Vogue in September 2026. “If my skin is going to be a little saggier than I would like, at least it looks dewy and pretty.”

But while she has she has gone through with the Botox, she won't bite the bullet on another popular procedure.

“I would love to have a buccal fat removal,” she added of the minor plastic surgery, where fat pads are removed from the lower cheeks for a slimmer look. “I can’t because everybody would know, but just know that I want that.”

“Oh, I’m really nervous about these fat transfers,” she noted. “I support other people doing them because I want to continue to watch and see what happens, but I don’t know about that.”

The Love Is Blind season three alum shared that she had gotten a boob job amid her divorce from husband Brennon Lemieux.

"I'm officially day five post-surgery and I feel pretty much back to normal for the most part," she shared in her January 2026 TikTok video. "I did a lift and an implant. Recovery hasn't been as tough as I thought that it would be. This is a surgery that I have been wanting to do for quite some time now, really, since I stopped breastfeeding my daughter. My girls just never set the same as they did before."

The Real Housewives of Orange County star treated herself to an early 50th birthday present in 2026 by going under the knife for a mini-facelift.

"My kids and husband all fought me on this decision saying 'mom/wife you don't need it, please don't do it, what can we do to talk you out of it," she recounted on Instagram. "But look at the results!!!! And now my husband and kids are all so happy with the results!!!!!! And truth is, it's MY decision, not theirs."

"I'm  loving every minute of my next decade and my 'refresh'!!!!!!!!" Alexis added. "It's subtle, but it's AMAZING!!!!"

The Real Housewives of Rhode Island star debuted a new look during the Bravo series' season one reunion, whiched aired in June 2026.

"After 25 years of debate," Rulla shared, "I finally decided to go ahead and get my rhinoplasty and a very minuscule lip lift while I was at it."

The Uncut Gems actress shared that she sometimes regrets the reasons she underwent her past cosmetic surgeries, which include liposuction, a rhinoplasty, veneers, Botox and fillers.

“When I see someone and I can tell they've never done anything,” she told Allure in August 2025, “I wish I could go back and be that person. I was so hung up on this idea that I needed to be attractive to men so that I could survive.”

Still, she admitted, “I probably will [get more work done one day], but I'm just not as concerned with it right now.”

The Real Housewives of Atlanta alum reversed her under-eye filler—which she got right after turning 18—on E!'s makeover series Botched Presents: Plastic Surgery Rewind.

"My skin is tighter," the reality star noted during the July 2025 episode. "I feel more youthful, more beautiful, more confident than ever before."

The 90 Day Fiancé alum debuted a jaw-dropping transformation after deciding to remove her gigantic breast implants on the July 30, 2025 episode of E!'s makeover series Botched Presents: Plastic Surgery Rewind.

"This reversal has been one of the most liberating and healing decisions I’ve ever made," Larissa exclusively told E! News after downsizing from 1,500 cc implants to 700 cc implants.. "It feels like I reclaimed a part of myself that I had put aside for the sake of an image, for expectations that weren’t truly mine."

The Shark Tank star shared a laundry list of plastic surgery and cosmetic procedures she's undergone over the years in a June 2025 Instagram post.

The Watch What Happens Live host, who had been open through the years about never getting Botox, revealed in March 2025 that he had embarked on his cosmetic journey and finally got the injectable procedure, which aims to reduce wrinkles.

"I just got it for the first time in my life," he said during the season 11 reunion episode of Married to Medicine. "About a month ago. They gave me a little."

The That's So Raven alum underwent a breast reduction surgery as a teen, a procedure she went on to regret.

"I should have done it after puberty," Raven-Symoné shared on a 2026 episode of the Allure Perspectives podcast. "I mean, they still look good, but it was hastily done. I wish I was stronger to say no."

According to the former Disney Channel star, adults around her at the time had told her that she "needed to do it in order to get a show."

"At the same time, I was like, 'If you're going to take my boobs out, I want lipo,'" she said in a 2025 episode of her Tea Time podcast. "Because when you gain weight, those boobs come back no matter what."

After years of denying cosmetic procedures, the lifestyle expert confessed in a February 2024 episode of her eponymous podcast that she gets Botox, fillers and lasers to tighten her skin. "I don't think a lot about age," she explained, "but I don't want to look my age."

The One Tree Hill alum discussed her cosmetic procedures—including Botox and getting breast implants—on her Whine Down podcast in February 2024. During the episode, she confessed her one qualm about her boob job.

“My biggest regret with my boobs is that I don't know if I solely did it for me,” Jana said. “My biggest piece of advice is it has to be 100 percent for you.”

In a Vanity Fair video released September 2024, the Wicked actress shared, "I've had fillers in various places and Botox, but I stopped like, four years ago. And that is the extent."

The Teen Mom 2 alum, a mother of seven, underwent a Brazlian butt lift and tummy tuck in 2016, and another tummy tuck, liposuction and breast reduction surgery in December 2024.

A month later, she spoke candidly about wrestling with her body image.

"I pray that my kids never struggle with their body images enough to mutilate their bodies to be skinny," she said on Instagram. "I think a little nip and tuck in terms of a nose job, or like a boob job is OK. But to go through this to be skinny is mental illness, truly. And I say that with the most respect to anyone going through it."

Blanchard underwent a rhinoplasty and septoplasty (nose job) in April 2024, three months after she was released from prison (where she served seven years for her role in the murder of her mother Clauddine "Dee Dee" Blanchard).

The Real Housewives of Dubai star publicly documented her November 2023 face lift and the recovery on social media.

"I wanted people to see how, when you come out, the scars and the cuts and what it really looks like," she exclusively told E! News of the procedure. "I literally looked like I'd been in a car crash and the car had won, but five days later you're presentable. Ten days later I was in a restaurant completely fine."

As for why the Bravo star was so open about her face lift journey? As she noted, "Being on a reality TV show, obviously it's going to look weird if I come back next season looking 10 years younger, which I do, obviously."

Part of the price of beauty for the "Who Says" singer: The occasional dabble with Botox.

The former Bravo star has been candid about her plastic surgery procedures in the past, including getting a nose job, having breast implants and dabbling with Botox and filler. And in 2024, she turned to CellSound's body sculpting treatment to tighten her stomach.

"I have actual abs," she told People in an interview published March 2024. "I have lines on my stomach that I haven't had since before I got pregnant. I think any mother knows after kids the elasticity of your skin will never be the same."

She also revealed in April 2025 that she's spent over $113,000 seeking treatment for a mysterious facial parasite.

Responding to an Instagram user who accused the Vanderpump Rules star of getting lip filler, Botox, jawline contouring with liposuction and eyelid surgery, Madix clapped back by confirming all of her past cosmetic procedures.

“i’ll tell you what i’ve had!” she wrote on Instagram in July 2024. “you’re partially correct. tox in 11’s, outer brow, and my neck. ellevate for my neck in 2019 by @theneckdoctor minimal lip filler bc my face is too small to handle very much and filler in my chin. absolutely no filler anywhere else and def no bleph yet. hope this helps! i’ll keep yall posted if i do anything else.”

"I'm bravely sharing that I had a lower facelift and a couple other minor tweaks," Zarin said in a June 2024 Instagram video, with a black bandage wrapped around her head. "I had a fat transplant put into my hands because I hated my hands, and the worst part was the lipo coming out of my leg to fill my hands. Believe it or not, that's the most pain I've had."

The Valley star revealed she underwent facial liposuction before filming the Bravo spinoff.

"I had work done on my double chin. We call it the turkey gobbler, runs in my family," she said on the March 2024 episode of her When Reality Hits podcast. "No matter what I was going through, no matter how much weight I lost, I still felt I had something there."

Following her breakup from Stranger Things' David Harbour, the "Smile" singer revealed she got "additions" in the way of a boob job.

"They look really incredible when I take my top off and my bra off," she shared on a March 2025 episode of her Miss Me? podcast. "But there's definitely a contrast in age between my breasts and my face."

The Beverly Hills, 90210 star has spoken publicly about her nose job and her breast implants.

In addition to getting candid on using Ozempic for weight loss, the talk show host admitted that her 2021 facelift was "the worst thing that I ever did," explaining in December 2023, "I looked like Cyclops."

"I've never had any work-work done, but I went through a phase when I was smoking pot when I was really obsessed with getting facial injections," the "Born This Way" singer told radio host Howard Stern in 2013. "I was going to this strip mall in Chicago in the back…Everybody was like, 'You are a nut job.'...I'm telling you, I wasn't exactly in the best frame of mind, and I would smoke a bunch of joints and have some drinks and I would be like, 'Oh, let's go see my girl' and we would drive to this strip mall and I would get shot up with a bunch of whatever, Juvéderm, and then leave."

She continued, "Now all the stuff is gone. Before I shot the 'Applause' video, [a photographer friend] was like, 'Gaga, I love you but if you don't stop injecting s--t in your face I'm going to just kill you.'"

The Real Housewives of New York star got breast implants in 2005, but removed them in 2008.

"Now I feel comfortable," she told Life & Style. "If there's something you're not comfortable with and you can correct it, great."

The Crown star revealed that she's a fan of Botox. "I've had loads," the actress told BBC Radio 2.

In 2013, The Talk co-host revealed on the show that she got plastic surgery at the beginning of her career in order to make her eyes look bigger.

"And after I had it done, the ball did roll for me," she said. "And I wondered, did I give in to the man?"

She added, "I have to live with every decision that I've made. And it got me to where we are today. And I'm not going to look back."

"I've done it all," the actress told The Telegraph in 2002. "I've had a little plastic surgery. I've had a little lipo. I've had a little Botox. And you know what? None of it works. None of it."

"I had [a deviated septum] fixed—best thing I ever did," the actress told People in 2007. "I slept like a baby for the first time in years. As far as all the other [rumors], as boring as it sounds, it's still mine. All of it. Still mine."

#806. Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?

Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

1987: Maradona stars in FA Centenary all-star game

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around Â£250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning Â£100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Soren Colding still has the shirt he wore for the Europe XI almost 30 years ago

#805. Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd

Rooney scored 53 goals in 120 appearances for England

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

#804. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much."

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it."

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid."

A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he said. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid."

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches."

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast

The new computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research shows that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore said. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day."

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.
