SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13. Starship will fly from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the 'jellyfish') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system. Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station, but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above, Star Dash, Orbital Radar and Find Starlink.

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Editor's Note: If you capture a photo of Starship and want to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

#788. Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

Some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages. Scientists have discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to make parchment, opening a new window into the 3,500-year history of sheeppox virus (SPPV).

The discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD). By analyzing parchment from centuries-old documents, the researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that this destructive disease was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times.

Sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, while also causing major economic losses by reducing wool, meat, and milk production.

Ancient Manuscripts Preserve the DNA of Deadly Viruses

Published in Science Advances, the new study reconstructs more than 3,500 years of sheeppox virus evolution. Researchers identified viral DNA in several historically important medieval manuscripts, revealing that documents preserved for their cultural significance can also contain valuable biological evidence.

Among the manuscripts examined was the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The researchers also studied older works, including the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, along with other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe.

The secret lies in the parchment itself. Before paper became widely available, manuscripts were often produced using carefully prepared animal hides, including skins from sheep, goats, and cattle. These materials can preserve traces of an animal's biological history, including evidence of infections present when it died.

In several manuscripts, the researchers detected sheeppox virus DNA on multiple pages. These findings indicate that infected animals had supplied some of the skins used to produce the documents.

An especially surprising discovery involved viral DNA found on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Because sheeppox primarily infects sheep, the results raise two possibilities: the virus may occasionally have infected other livestock species, or viral material may have contaminated the skins during parchment production.

Historic Books Become Unexpected Disease Archives

"The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," said Louis L'Hôte, PhD candidate at UCD and lead author of the study.

"These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies -- such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia."

The findings suggest that libraries and archives may hold far more information about historical diseases than previously recognized. Manuscripts that have survived for hundreds of years could provide genetic evidence of livestock outbreaks that left few other records.

"Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained. This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period," said Dr. Kevin G. Daly, Associate Professor at UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science and the study's supervising author.

"This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data -- a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on."

The project brought together specialists in genetics, history, virology, protein chemistry, and conservation, allowing the team to investigate the manuscripts from both historical and biological perspectives.

Ancient Sheep Teeth Reveal 3,700 Years of Disease

The medieval manuscripts were only part of the investigation. To trace the disease further into the past, the scientists also examined DNA recovered from sheep teeth dating to the Bronze Age.

Teeth are particularly useful for studying ancient infections because they can protect genetic material for thousands of years, often preserving evidence that has disappeared from other skeletal remains.

The researchers identified the oldest known genetic traces of sheeppox virus in sheep teeth recovered from ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe. When combined with the manuscript findings, this evidence shows that the disease has affected livestock for more than 3,700 years.

To investigate how the virus developed, the team compared ancient viral DNA with genetic sequences from modern viruses. Their analysis suggests that the main branches of the capripoxvirus family (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) separated from one another sometime between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.

That estimated timeline coincides with major changes in human history, including the domestication of livestock and the large-scale movement of sheep from the Eurasian steppe into Europe. These movements may have played an important role in the virus's long history of transmission.

A Deadly Virus That Has Barely Changed in Thousands of Years

One of the study's most striking findings was how little the sheeppox virus has changed genetically over the past several thousand years. Unlike some other viruses, its genome appears to have remained remarkably stable despite its long history of infecting livestock.

Understanding that stability could help scientists identify the genetic changes that originally allowed the virus to become an effective sheep pathogen.

The discovery also has immediate relevance. Sheeppox remains a serious threat to livestock farming, with outbreaks continuing to cause substantial economic damage.

"People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen -- there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," said Louis L'Hôte.

"Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia."

L'Hôte added: "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future."

By uncovering viral DNA in both medieval manuscripts and prehistoric animal remains, the researchers have demonstrated a powerful new way to investigate the history of infectious diseases. Their work suggests that materials preserved for entirely different purposes may contain valuable clues about the emergence, spread, and evolution of pathogens that continue to affect the world today.

The research was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council. Led by UCD, the project involved more than 30 institutions in Ireland and internationally, including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

Materials provided by University College Dublin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

#786. DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets

Scientists have uncovered a remarkable collection of DNA hidden within the Shroud of Turin, revealing a surprisingly complex biological history behind one of the world's most mysterious and controversial religious artifacts. The genetic evidence includes traces of humans, bacteria, fungi, plants, animals, and even Mediterranean red coral, offering new clues about the environments and people that have come into contact with the famous cloth over the centuries.

Published in Scientific Reports, the study used advanced DNA sequencing technology to examine samples collected from the Shroud in 1978. For the first time, researchers applied a sophisticated technique (rigorous PCR-free next-generation metagenomic sequencing) to these officially collected samples, allowing them to identify genetic material preserved within the linen fibers in unprecedented detail.

Unlike traditional DNA testing, which often focuses on genetic material from a single organism, metagenomic sequencing can detect DNA from many different species within the same sample. This makes it particularly useful for studying historical objects that have been handled, stored, and exposed to changing environments over long periods.

By examining this genetic material, the international research team assembled what they describe as the most comprehensive picture yet of the biological traces accumulated on the Shroud throughout its history.

Human DNA and a Hidden World of Microorganisms

Among the discoveries were multiple lineages of human mitochondrial DNA, suggesting that genetic material from different human populations has accumulated on the cloth. Mitochondrial DNA is a small portion of our genetic material that is inherited through the maternal line, making it especially useful for studying ancestry and population history.

The researchers also identified an unexpectedly diverse microbiome, the collection of microscopic organisms associated with a particular environment or object. These included bacteria commonly found on human skin, various fungi, and microorganisms adapted to living in salty environments.

Some of these organisms belong to a group known as archaea, which are single-celled microorganisms distinct from bacteria. Certain archaea can thrive in extremely salty conditions that would be difficult for many other forms of life to tolerate.

Together, these findings reveal that the Shroud carries a complicated biological record shaped by repeated human contact and exposure to different environmental conditions.

DNA From Plants, Animals, and Mediterranean Coral

The discoveries extended far beyond human DNA and microorganisms. Scientists also detected genetic traces from numerous plant and animal species, adding another layer to the Shroud's biological history.

Plant DNA included cultivated wheat, carrots, maize, bananas, and peanuts. Genetic material from domesticated animals was also present, including cattle, pigs, chickens, dogs, and cats.

One particularly unusual finding was DNA associated with Mediterranean red coral.

The wide variety of biological material suggests that the cloth has encountered a diverse range of living organisms and environmental influences. These genetic traces may reflect its long history of handling, storage, and movement through different geographical regions.

Importantly, the presence of DNA from a particular species does not establish when that material reached the cloth. Some traces could have accumulated relatively recently, while others may reflect much older interactions. This makes the findings valuable for reconstructing the Shroud's environmental history, but also highlights the difficulty of interpreting DNA recovered from an object that has been exposed to human activity for centuries.

Can DNA Solve the Mystery of the Shroud of Turin?

Despite the remarkable diversity of genetic material, the researchers emphasize that their findings cannot establish the Shroud's age or authenticity.

The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a human figure and has long been associated by some believers with the burial of Jesus. Its origins have been debated for generations, making it one of the most extensively investigated historical and religious artifacts in the world.

Because the cloth has been touched and exposed to different environments over many centuries, its DNA represents a mixture of biological material accumulated at different times. This makes it impossible to reliably separate any original DNA that might have been associated with the fabric from the many genetic traces deposited afterward.

Instead, the research demonstrates how modern forensic genomics and proteomics can reveal information that traditional methods might miss. Forensic genomics uses genetic evidence to investigate biological origins and interactions, while proteomics examines proteins, which can also preserve valuable clues about biological materials.

Together, these approaches offer powerful new ways to investigate how historical objects have been preserved, handled, and exposed to different environments.

Modern DNA Technology Reveals New Historical Clues

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, contributed to the international research collaboration. She emphasized that advances in forensic technology are making it possible to recover information from historical samples collected decades earlier.

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, said: "The Shroud of Turin continues to fascinate historians, scientists and the public, and we're thrilled to reveal new information about the biological complexity preserved within samples collected almost 50 years ago by applying new cutting-edge forensic DNA technologies.

"The Shroud represents a rich archive of genetic information that has accumulated over centuries of human interaction and environmental exposure. While the DNA evidence cannot answer all the questions about the age or authenticity of the cloth, it provides novel insights into its biological history and demonstrates how advances in forensic science can unlock new information from historical artifacts."

This supernova imposter erupts every 113 days as the compact object gets close to the unstable massive star.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered.

When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement.

Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation.

The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space.

However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed.

"To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said.

Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026.

Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst.

The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said.

Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable.

Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system.

Each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts.

As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw.

The X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova.

"We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," said team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical."

Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun, and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun.

Nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit. It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies.

AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list.

AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object.

The X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#783. Chris Rock Gushes to Kimmel About Inducting Wu-Tang Clan into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: ‘They Are the Top of the Top’

As far as Oasis is concerned, though, the Misty Green director understands that the Gallaghers are "too cool" for the RRHOF.

Chris Rock movingly introduced the Wu-Tang Clan at Saturday’s 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Los Angeles, and even days later the Misty Green writer/director/star was still floating on cloud nine about the whole thing.

Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn-bred Rock seemed to be still pinching himself over the honor of inducting the legendary Staten Island crew into the Hall of Fame. “I had the pleasure of doing that,” Rock told Jimmy Kimmel on Monday night (Nov. 16). “They’re the greatest, most incredible … the best group of all time,” he continued, running out of superlatives.

Then he found another one. “The worst guy in the Wu-Tang is better than every rapper you know,” Rock stated. “They are the top of the top.” Kimmel and Rock then discussed the logistics of such an expansive group getting microphone time to say their thanks yous, describing group musical mastermind RZA going up first, followed by Method Man, another member of the group and then … a cut microphone.

“Because there’s nine guys,” Kimmel explained of the group that also includes GZA, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Masta Killa and Cappadonna. “I had nothing to do with that,” Rock assured any disgruntled Wu-Tang fans. “There’s a lot of Wu in the house.”

The men also discussed the long list of no-shows for the ceremony, including Oasis, who very pointedly declined the invitation. “Oasis can’t come,” Rock said, stating the obvious. “They’re too cool. You would have been mad if they came.” Kimmel noted that British heavy metal icons Iron Maiden also skipped out. “Well, they’re old,” Rock suggested. “They’re like Rusty Maiden now.”

“To me, the message is ‘we’re cooler than the Wu-Tang Clan,'” Kimmel said of Oasis and Iron Maiden’s decision to no-show. “If the Wu-Tang Clan can come, everybody else can show up.”

#782. Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images

The Milky Way is believed to contain billions of planets beyond our solar system. These distant worlds, known as exoplanets, offer astronomers an opportunity to explore other planetary systems, identify potentially habitable environments, and perhaps eventually discover evidence of life elsewhere in the universe.

Finding these planets is one challenge. Actually seeing them is another. Most exoplanets orbit stars that shine so brightly that the planets become nearly impossible to distinguish from the surrounding glare. Even the most advanced space telescopes struggle to separate the faint light of a distant planet from the overwhelming brightness of its host star.

Now, researchers have developed a powerful new method for removing that starlight from telescope images, revealing planets that were previously hidden. The technique uses a sophisticated computer simulation of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and has already exposed an exoplanet that was concealed in existing observations. In tests involving known planets, it achieved two to 15 times greater detection sensitivity than conventional approaches.

A Digital Twin of James Webb Reveals Hidden Planets

The breakthrough centers on a virtual replica of Webb's Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), an instrument designed to observe the universe in infrared light. By recreating how the camera operates, researchers can identify and correct tiny imperfections that interfere with its observations.

The virtual model, often called a "digital twin," allows scientists to simulate the telescope's behavior and determine how starlight spreads through its optical system. Once they understand the patterns produced by the star, they can digitally subtract much of that glare, making faint planets easier to detect.

"Directly imaging exoplanets is incredibly challenging because even the tiniest imperfections in a telescope can make it difficult to separate the faint light of a planet from the overwhelming glare of its star," explains Caltech's Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy, a Rosenberg Scholar, and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, who is a co-author of a Nature paper about the new method published online November 4.

"What's exciting is that we're showing how computation can help overcome limitations of the telescope itself," Bouman continues. "By combining a physical model of the instrument with optimization techniques from machine learning, we have been able to remove starlight much more precisely, making it easier to detect faint exoplanets and even reveal one that was previously hidden in the JWST data."

How Scientists Make Blinding Starlight Disappear

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Rather than relying entirely on improvements to telescope hardware, the system uses advanced computation to correct problems in images that have already been collected.

To develop FLIP, the team created a detailed physical model of Webb's infrared camera. They then used computational techniques to examine millions of possible imperfections, subtle changes, and other unknown factors that could influence the telescope's observations.

These small variations matter because even an extremely slight distortion can alter how a star appears in an image. When astronomers attempt to remove the star's light, any remaining glare can overwhelm the much dimmer signal from a nearby planet.

By accounting for these effects, FLIP produces a highly precise model of the star's appearance. Researchers can then subtract that modeled starlight from the original observations, allowing previously obscured objects to become visible.

"This is the first time that we have demonstrated that these little imperfections or instabilities are not a limiting factor in the kinds of planets we can image," says lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a graduate student at Northwestern University in the lab of astronomer Jason Wang, who is also a co-author of the paper. "As you go through this iterative process of trying to find what the telescope actually is doing during observations, you basically see the glare of the star disappearing in very bizarre ways. It gets dimmer and very deformed until at the end you get a pretty clean image and, if you're lucky, there's a blob there, which is a glowing planet."

A Failed Experiment Led to a Major Breakthrough

The idea behind FLIP began taking shape when Ferrer-Chavez was an undergraduate student at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in Mexico. He had already participated in a Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship project with Wang, who was then a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow (named after the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like star) in the laboratory of Dimitri Mawet.

Mawet is the David Morrisroe Professor of Astronomy at Caltech and a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech. He also serves as director of instrumentation for the Caltech Optical Observatories.

At the time, Ferrer-Chavez was looking for additional opportunities to pursue research. Meanwhile, Wang had been discussing a potential collaboration with Bouman that would combine her expertise in computational imaging with his knowledge of astronomical instruments. Their shared goal was to improve the ability of telescopes to directly image exoplanets.

The two researchers brought Ferrer-Chavez into the project and began mentoring him. However, the initial effort did not produce the results they had hoped for.

"Rodrigo's senior thesis was an exploration of possible approaches, none of which ended up being what we did for this paper, but it helped rule out what not to do and also helped us understand the problem better," Wang says. "I believe our recent success was only possible because we did that exercise first."

Ferrer-Chavez originally attempted to train machine learning models to predict the patterns of starlight appearing in telescope data. That strategy proved unsuccessful, prompting the team to rethink how the technology could be used.

Instead of asking artificial intelligence to predict what the glare should look like, they turned to computational tools developed for machine learning to perform detailed physical calculations.

These methods allowed the researchers to adjust millions of variables, much like turning an enormous collection of control knobs. Each adjustment helped refine their simulation of the telescope until it more closely reproduced the actual observations. Performing this many calculations manually would be impractical.

The resulting approach combines the physical laws governing light and telescope optics with the computational power of modern optimization methods. Rather than simply guessing what should be removed from an image, FLIP uses a model of how the telescope produces that image in the first place.

James Webb's Archives May Contain More Hidden Worlds

One of the most exciting possibilities is that astronomers may not need new telescope observations to benefit from the discovery.

Webb has already collected enormous amounts of astronomical data, including images of stars that could harbor planets too faint to detect using earlier analysis methods. FLIP offers a way to revisit these observations and search for objects that were overlooked.

"We now have a tool that lets us discover and study planets that we were not able to 'see' before, even if that planet was already in an image in the JWST archive," Ferrer-Chavez explains. "We can try to find planets that may have been missed there, and also planets that perhaps we tried to image, but we could not actually detect at the time."

This means some planets that were previously considered beyond the reach of direct imaging could potentially be identified without sending another telescope into space.

It also changes how astronomers can think about existing observations. An image that appears to contain nothing but a brilliant star may hold additional information about planets hidden beneath its glare.

Pushing Telescopes Beyond Their Physical Limits

Astronomers have spent decades developing technology to reduce the overwhelming brightness of stars. One important tool is a coronagraph, an instrument designed to block starlight so that faint objects nearby can be observed more clearly.

For example, NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope carries a Coronagraph Instrument developed by researchers at Caltech, JPL, and IPAC (a science and data center for astronomy at Caltech). The instrument is specifically designed to suppress starlight and improve the direct imaging of exoplanets.

But even exceptionally precise telescope hardware has unavoidable limitations. Wang explains that physical instruments alone cannot match the level of correction achieved by FLIP when processing the images.

"The James Webb Space Telescope, which we demonstrated on, is optically stable to the nanometer level, which just sounds pretty awesome, but that's still limiting," he says. "We're excited because this technique is not limited specifically to JWST. Because of some very specific design, this technique could be used on any telescope."

A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, meaning Webb's optical system maintains extraordinary precision. Yet even disturbances on this incredibly small scale can interfere with the detection of planets next to bright stars.

FLIP offers a different way around that problem. Instead of requiring the telescope itself to eliminate every tiny imperfection, the technique mathematically accounts for those effects after the observations have been made.

The researchers now intend to refine FLIP and investigate how it could work with additional instruments, including the Roman Space Telescope and telescopes operating from Earth's surface.

A Powerful New Tool in the Search for Another Earth

The implications may extend well beyond today's observatories. The researchers believe their approach could help shape future space missions, particularly those designed to search for planets resembling Earth.

One major possibility is NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The mission is intended to become the first telescope specifically designed to search for evidence of life on planets orbiting other stars.

A central objective would be to photograph Earth-like planets within the habitable zones of stars similar to our Sun. A habitable zone is the range of distances around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface, assuming suitable atmospheric conditions.

But the technical challenge is enormous. An Earth-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star can be approximately 10 billion times fainter than the star itself, making the planet extraordinarily difficult to distinguish from the surrounding light.

"The goal of HWO is to find Earth-like planets and the habitable zones of Sun-like stars through a direct imaging method," Ferrer-Chavez says. "The engineering challenge of trying to image something that is around 10 billion times fainter than something right next to it is a brutal -- not just to clean the image but to build a telescope that can take that image."

FLIP could make that challenge more manageable. If astronomers can digitally remove more unwanted starlight after capturing an image, future telescope designs may not need to overcome every source of optical instability through hardware alone.

The approach could therefore give engineers greater flexibility while allowing astronomers to extract more information from the light their instruments collect.

"I feel we just unlocked a new frontier," Wang says. "We've now gone beyond the telescope stability limit for the first time with this new technique, and this new paradigm, I think, can be applied to every instrument that's trying to image exoplanets."

Bringing the Search for Alien Life Into Focus

For Bouman, the long-term ambition is much larger than simply finding more distant planets. Astronomers ultimately hope to obtain direct images of worlds resembling Earth and examine them for possible signs of life.

Reaching that goal will require major advances in telescope engineering, astronomical instruments, and image processing. But the new research demonstrates that some of the most important improvements may come from better ways of interpreting data rather than building increasingly precise hardware.

"There's still a long way to go, but this work shows how much more is possible when we combine advances in telescope technology with computational imaging," Bouman says. "Sometimes, the key to seeing something new isn't just building a better instrument but finding a better way to make sense of the light it collects."

The findings were published in Nature in a paper titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit." Additional co-authors include William T. Freeman and Brandon Y. Feng of MIT, along with Laurent Pueyo and Marshall D. Perrin of the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore.

The research received support from the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Sloan Foundation, an Amazon AI4Science Discovery Award, and the National Science Foundation.

James Gunn's new DC universe might be done, but the follow-up to 2025's Superman is still on the way.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman, the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out, and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU.

That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor's return.

Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU.

Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday, Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground.

We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow.

Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time.

Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen.

Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first.

When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is.

With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027.

Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max:

Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/yearStandard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year

No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas.

Yes, James Gunn has officially confirmed Brainiac is the main threat Earth is facing in Man of Tomorrow. This explains why other heroes will be joining Superman in a fight against the alien mastermind, but the plot is looking a bit more complex.

In typical comic book fashion (and somewhat reminiscent of Thor: The Dark World), the main hook in Man of Tomorrow appears to be a reluctant alliance between the first movie's villain, Lex Luthor, and Kal-El (aka Clark Kent). "Enemies to allies" is always a fun dynamic to have in a sequel, especially when stars David Corenswet (Superman) and Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) delivered strong and memorable performances the first time around.

The actual plot remains under wraps, but we can guess Brainiac — one of DC's biggest and most iconic alien villains — will be a tough nut to crack, thus requiring some sort of unofficial team-up that will include returning heroes like Mister Terrific, Guy Gardner, Hawkgirl, John Stewart, Blue Beetle, and even Kara Zor-El (Supergirl). There are other names circling the project that could lead to even bigger appearances, but don't expect to learn much about them before the movie's marketing kicks off.

Why should you care about Brainiac? Well, he's a super-intelligent techno-organic alien from the planet Colu with an obsession with knowledge and self-improvement. A perfect foe for Luthor, Earth's greatest mind, but also a breath of fresh air for Superman, who's been stuck battling either Kryptonian menaces or just Luthor too long on the big screen.

As a direct continuation of Superman, Man of Tomorrow is bringing back plenty of actors in both main and supporting roles, including:

New cast members with publicly announced (or previously established) characters include:

Last but not least, we also know Adria Arjona, Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls are part of the cast, but their parts remain a secret for now.

Much of the current Man of Tomorrow speculation centers on Adria Arjona's role in the story. While many have theorized she could be playing Wonder Woman — something that neither Gunn nor Arjona has straight-up denied — the earlier reports and rumors suggested she could be Maxima.

Such a role would fit Gunn's penchant for throwing lesser-known comic book heroes and villains into his movies wherever possible. If you're not an avid reader or longtime DC fan, all you need to know is that Maxima is an alien conqueror from the planet Almerac obsessed with Superman as her perfect mate and king. She's also morally ambiguous, at least when she first appeared, so that makes her a particularly interesting character to bring in for a more complex and nuanced sequel.

With Brainiac spearheading the roster of new DC icons joining Man of Tomorrow, it also isn't hard to imagine another alien figure factoring into the plot, though the flick is getting extremely crowded as it is.

Yes, James Gunn is the sole writer and director of Man of Tomorrow.

Despite his previous role as co-chairman and co-CEO of DC Studios, Gunn is extremely hands-on when it comes to most DCU projects. In fact, it seems he had already begun working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, though his unceremonious exit will almost certainly mean the end of those plans.

He's also co-producing alongside Peter Safran, who was also ousted in November 2026's DC Studios shakeup.

The rest of the crew includes Sam McCurdy (Peacemaker, Shogun) as cinematographer, Fred Raskin (Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Supergirl) as editor, and David Fleming (Superman, Anaconda) as the main composer, among others.

#778. The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

A neuron from the human hippocampus. The bushy branches receive signals from other neurons. Credit: Jake Watson and Rebecca Morse-Mora, Jonas group, ISTA

Neuroscientist Lucy Palmer and her team have been waiting days for this moment.

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more

Across the road from her laboratory, at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia, surgeons are removing brain tissue from a person with brain cancer. They set some aside for Palmer to collect and study. It is about the size of a shelled peanut.

A colleague of hers takes the sample, places it in a tub of artificial cerebrospinal fluid and rushes it back to the lab, securing it in a chamber filled with bubbling carbon dioxide and oxygen to keep it alive.

These precious samples can survive for only a day or so before they start to deteriorate, so Palmer’s team wastes no time. Within half an hour of receiving the tissue, they are recording the electrical current passing between neurons as they fire.

Palmer’s group at the Florey Institute in Melbourne is using live brain tissue to understand more about brain cancers and how the activity of neurons influences tumour growth. Her lab, and others using such samples, are doing something rare — measuring how live, working human neurons behave.

Most studies of brain-cell function rely on tissue taken from people who have died or from living animals. Post-mortem human brains, however, preserve only the structure and not the activity of cells, and the brains of other animals might function differently. “As much as we like mice, I don’t want to understand the mouse brain. I want to understand the human brain,” Palmer says.

Slices from a sample of living human brain ready for study.Credit: Emmalyn P. Leonard

Working with living brain tissue from another person is both humbling and a great privilege, she says. “Every sample is precious.” It’s also an artisanal skill: attaching recording equipment to individual neurons requires the neuroscientific equivalent of a gardener’s green fingers. It relies on mastery of a decades-old technique called patch-clamping, which has fallen out of fashion as flashier recording methods have become available.

Despite the barriers, there is increasing interest in this rare resource. The number of studies published about this tissue has increased from just a handful two decades ago to upwards of 40 a year, according to data from Scopus, with the bulk attributed to about ten research teams. Neuroscientists around the world are working with surgeons to access the tissue and keep it alive in their labs for periods of time ranging from 24 hours to a few weeks, investigating the intrinsic electrical properties of cells and how they communicate with each other during both health and disease.

“When looking into a disease, being able to look directly at the human tissue is absolutely vital,” says Palmer.

Neuroscientists have many ways to study the human brain: non-invasive scanning, indirect measures such as blood samples and, after death, in slices under the microscope. They can also study brain function directly in animal models and, very rarely, in people who have electrodes implanted while they are undergoing surgery. But none of those approaches allows scientists to measure and manipulate the activity of individual human brain cells in their natural environment.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture

That has changed in the past ten years, says Scott Owen, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. Although people have been studying live human tissue since the 1970s, he says, the field has finally reached a point at which enough is known about the mammalian brain to understand how human brains differ from those of other animals.

His team works with paediatric neurosurgeons to acquire tissue taken from children with epilepsy, cancer or abnormal tangles of blood vessels in their brains. By comparing samples from people with different diseases, the researchers can look for features common to all donors and deduce which are conserved properties of the human brain, rather than artefacts of any one condition.

In a preprint published in September, for instance, Owen and his colleagues found distinct differences in how human pyramidal neurons — big, bushy brain cells that live in the cortex — mature compared with those of mice1. The team analysed neocortex samples from 24 children and teenagers, ranging in age from 9 months to 18 years, and mouse samples from equivalent developmental stages. The study, which is yet to be peer reviewed, looked at patterns in how neurons fire, or spike. It’s known that human neurons are quicker to spike after a stimulus than are rodent neurons and that this might correlate with intelligence. Owen and his colleagues found that human neurons got faster at responding over the course of development, with neurons from teens spiking more quickly than those from children; the opposite happened in mice.

Slices from a sample of living human brain, ready for study.Credit: Rennie Kendrick

When the researchers looked at the genes that might explain how this happens, they found two that increased in expression over time in people, but not in mice. These genes help to create ion channels in cell membranes, which allows signals to travel between neurons. Faults in these genes have been linked to several neurodevelopmental conditions2.

Karri Lämsä, a biophysicist at the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine in Szeged, is also interested in how human neurons fire and how these patterns might change with time and new experiences. His team studies centimetre-wide cubes of the cortex that are discarded during surgeries to enable access to deeper parts of the brain. In a study published last year, they looked at a type of neuron that inhibits others. In these cells, the axon — the main trunk — transmits signals faster and spikes at lower thresholds than in the same cells in mice3. Fast-acting neurons of this type are thought to have a crucial role in complex brain functions.

Lämsä’s team has also been studying how networks of these fast-spiking neurons might change with age. In samples taken from 106 people ranging in age from 11 to 84 years, the researchers found that these circuits become weaker over time and the spikes in electricity travelling across the cell membrane become smaller and slower4. These changes could explain why the human brain becomes less capable of learning and processing information as people age.

Other work using live human tissue has challenged a key assumption about the human brain: that it is a scaled-up version of the mouse brain. Peter Jonas, a neuroscientist at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria in Klosterneuburg, is using live human tissue to understand how brain cells function alone and in networks. Jonas had worked with animal models for more than 30 years when, in 2022, he began collaborating with a neurosurgeon at the Medical University of Vienna. He would receive tiny samples of human brain tissue — mainly from the hippocampus — measuring about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle

Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle

His lab’s work suggests that some properties of the human brain, such as the number of dendritic spines (tiny outgrowths at the end of synapses that connect neurons), follow different scaling rules from those of the mouse. Neurons are also more densely connected in the human neocortex — the area of the brain thought to control higher functions such as decision-making and planning — than in the mouse one, but have fewer connections in the hippocampus. Jonas says that this kind of information can be gleaned only from living tissue.

In a 2025 Cell study examining tissue taken from the hippocampus and cortex, his team also found that the electrical signals transmitted between neurons were more reliable and precise than they were in mouse brains5. The synapses in human brains successfully triggered the receiving cell to fire 90% of the time, compared with a 62% success rate in mice. Computer modelling by Jonas’s team suggests that reliable transmission could set the human brain apart from those of other species. “We are at the beginning of understanding this,” says Jonas.

Meanwhile, Palmer has observed that the excitability of brain cells differs between humans and rodents6, which could be because human dendrites are twice as wide as those of mice. Differences in size also affect how the cells handle information, she says. Larger neurons with longer, bushier branches can form widespread networks, whereas smaller neurons restrict a network to their close neighbours.

Palmer also finds human tissue invaluable for studying disease. Cancers in mouse brains are generally composed of a limited number of cell types, whereas every single cell in a human brain tumour is different. Furthermore, most brain cancer research in mice has focused on one particular type of cancer, called glioblastoma.

Neurons from the human cortex next to their neighbours. Scientists can record from several branches of these complex neurons to monitor their activity.Credit: Jake Watson, Jonas group, ISTA

Using slices of human brain tissue, Palmer and her team have found that cancer cells taken from aggressive tumours were more active than those in slower growing tumours7, boosting signalling and forming more synapses with neurons. The researchers also found that neurons were generally more active in people with aggressive tumours and that this increased activity leads to greater spread of cancer cells, confirming results from animal models.

In a study testing the efficacy of a drug for brain cancer, Palmer’s team also saw changes to excitability and signalling in neurons8. Together, the findings could explain how the drug slows down tumour growth, or halts it entirely.

One of the biggest challenges of working with living human brain tissue is a specialist technique that scientists need to learn. Called patch-clamping, the technique involves pressing the tip of a glass micropipette against the membrane surrounding a neuron and using suction to make a tight seal. A cell’s electrical activity can then be measured through one or several ion channels in the membrane. These measurements are used to study how a neuron behaves in response to different stimuli.

Patch-clamping was invented in the 1970s and is an indispensable tool in electrophysiology. It stands in stark contrast to techniques such as calcium imaging and optical imaging, which allow scientists to measure electrical activity in thousands of neurons at once. These techniques are more expensive but less technically challenging, says Palmer. In comparison, “patch-clamping takes a year to learn and years to understand,” she says. “You never master it.”

Liftoff is scheduled for 5:45 p.m. ET today (Nov. 13).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #776. A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought

A radical alternative to the standard picture of the cosmos is gaining attention after researchers at the University of Ottawa reported that it successfully matched several important astronomical observations. The model suggests that the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old, nearly twice the widely accepted age of 13.8 billion years, and that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed to explain its behavior.

If further research supports these findings, the theory could offer a very different explanation for how the Universe evolved. It may also help resolve one of modern astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the existence of surprisingly large and mature galaxies at a time when the conventional model suggests they should barely have begun forming.

Throughout 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras evaluated an alternative cosmological framework known as CCC+TL against several major astronomical observations.

The name stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” Rather than relying on dark matter and dark energy, the model proposes that some of the effects attributed to these mysterious components could result from changes over time in fundamental physical constants. These constants help determine how particles and forces interact.

For decades, astronomers have searched for direct evidence of dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter is thought to provide additional gravity that helps explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures hold together. Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the Universe to accelerate. Although extensive observations support their gravitational and cosmological effects, neither component has been directly identified.

The prevailing cosmological framework, called ΛCDM, incorporates both. Despite its success in explaining a wide range of observations, it faces questions raised by the discovery of unexpectedly developed galaxies in the early Universe.

“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Professor Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”

Testing such a fundamentally different theory requires more than adjusting the standard model. CCC+TL modifies the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and how the Universe expands. As a result, Gupta and Samaras had to develop equations and computer programs specifically adapted to their model for each test.

The researchers report that CCC+TL produced results consistent with several major astronomical measurements. One important test involved the light elements created shortly after the Big Bang, including hydrogen and helium. The alternative model predicted abundances that matched those calculated using the standard cosmological framework.

It also agreed with cosmic chronometer measurements, which allow astronomers to reconstruct the history of cosmic expansion by comparing the ages of galaxies at different distances. These measurements provide an independent way to examine how the expansion rate has changed over billions of years.

Another significant test focused on the motion of galaxies. In a recent study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers examined all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database. They found that their model could reproduce the observed rotation curves without invoking dark matter.

Rotation curves describe how quickly stars and gas orbit at different distances from the centers of galaxies. Under conventional gravity, the visible matter alone generally cannot explain these motions, which is one of the major reasons scientists believe dark matter exists.

The team also investigated time dilation in observations of supernovae. Time dilation refers to the apparent stretching of events over time when viewed across vast cosmic distances. Their analysis offered additional support for CCC+TL, although the research paper remains under review.

The researchers also examined the Bullet Cluster, a famous system of colliding galaxy clusters that provides some of the strongest observational evidence for dark matter.

In this system, most of the ordinary matter is concentrated in extremely hot gas that emits X-rays. However, observations show that much of the gravitational effect is associated with the galaxies rather than the gas. The standard explanation is that invisible dark matter passed through the collision along with the galaxies.

Under CCC+TL, the additional gravitational effect predicted by the model also follows the galaxies instead of the hot gas, but without requiring dark matter. The researchers emphasize that this result is only an initial proof of concept and that more detailed investigations are necessary.

“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” adds Professor Gupta, who examines this possibility further in a separate paper exploring the origin of dark matter and dark energy.

Perhaps the most intriguing implication of the model involves the earliest galaxies ever observed.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered galaxies that appear surprisingly massive and mature for their early place in cosmic history. Their existence has prompted questions about how quickly stars and galaxies could have formed after the Big Bang.

CCC+TL offers a possible answer by giving the early Universe substantially more time to develop.

In the standard cosmological model, the Universe was approximately 300 million years old during the period known as cosmic dawn, when the first generations of stars and galaxies were emerging. At the same observed redshift, however, CCC+TL would place the Universe's age at roughly 4.6 billion years.

Redshift measures how much light from a distant object has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers use it to study distant galaxies and investigate earlier stages of cosmic history.

Under the alternative model, galaxies observed at extremely high redshifts would have had billions of additional years to grow. The researchers calculate that early galaxies would be approximately 12 times larger in both size and mass than predicted by standard cosmology, according to findings published in Galaxies 13, 115.

“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Professor Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”

Upcoming observations could provide an important opportunity to investigate this prediction.

The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program aims to search for extremely distant galaxies, potentially reaching redshifts greater than 50. These observations would probe an exceptionally early period in the Universe's history under the standard cosmological framework.

According to conventional models, there may not have been enough time for large galaxies to assemble at such extreme redshifts. The CCC+TL model does not impose the same restriction because its cosmic timeline allows substantially more time for galaxies to develop.

Finding galaxies at these distances could therefore provide another important way to compare the competing explanations. However, such discoveries would not, by themselves, establish that the alternative model is correct.

Although the researchers report encouraging results across several major cosmological tests, CCC+TL remains an unconventional proposal that requires further independent examination. The standard cosmological model continues to explain a broad range of astronomical observations, and any replacement must ultimately demonstrate comparable or greater success.

For Gupta, the latest findings provide a reason to continue investigating the possibility that the Universe operates differently than scientists currently assume.

“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Professor Gupta.

Materials provided by University of Ottawa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#774. Felipe Holguín Appointed CEO of Universal Music Latin America and Iberian Peninsula

The Colombian executive takes over as the head of Universal's entire global Latin operation, including Brazil.

Felipe Holguín, an entrepreneur and executive whose experience has straddled music, media, technology and finance across countries and languages, has been named CEO of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula, effective immediately, the company announced Tuesday (Nov. 17). He will be based in Miami, reporting directly to Sir Lucian Grainge, chairman and CEO of UMG.

Holguín takes over as the head of UMG’s Latin operations, including Spain, Portugal and Brazil, after longtime CEO Jesús López announced Monday (Nov. 16) that he was stepping down from that post after nearly 30 years. López has taken on a new role as chairman emeritus of Global Talent Services (GTS).

Holguín doesn’t come directly from the music industry and hasn’t worked inside a label, but he has vast experience in building creative businesses and leading digital organizations.

“Latin music has led the way in opening global audiences to artists around the world, showing how music can cross borders while staying rooted in the cultures that give it life,” Grainge said in a press release. “Felipe combines deep respect for artistry and the Latin creative ecosystem with expertise across business, technology, and data. I’m excited to see him work with our teams to invest in the extraordinary and the unexpected and to create more global opportunities for artists.”

Holguin added: “Artists are the ultimate change agents. Our role is to bring together the ideas, platforms, and partnerships that help them reach fans and move culture forward. Jesús and the talented people across Latin America and Iberia have helped shape Latin music’s global rise. I’m excited to work with UMG’s teams across the globe to build our company around artists and help their music travel even further.”

“I’m proud to welcome Felipe to UMG,” said López. “He’s an accomplished leader with a clear vision for the future, and I’m confident he’ll build on the extraordinary foundation our teams have created.”

While not a former label exec, Holguin is known to those in the industry and has close ties in many sectors, particularly in the U.S. Latin market.

Born in Cali, Colombia, Holguín has an MBA from Harvard and his previous experience includes serving as CEO of Fusion Media Group inside Univision, where he applied a multi-language, multicultural approach. He was also executive vp of digital, news and music at Univision, overseeing all operations, including mergers and acquisitions, music streaming and the network’s televised award shows. Holguín later worked with Exile Content Studio on the launch, growth and sale of its music business to HYBE and its eventual acquisition by Candle Media. Most recently, he worked with HYBE Latin America on strategy and operations.

Holguín will begin his tenure at Universal’s Miami offices this week and will be working with both local and global teams at UMG to “help identify and develop the next generation of talent and support artists at every stage of their careers,” according to a press statement.
